item.title: GOP senators endure painful week with little to show for it
item.description:
Exhausted GOP senators are preparing to fly home mostly empty-handed after staying in D.C. longer than expected.

Why it matters: The midterm outlook is getting bleaker by the day, and Republicans have a monster to-do list for the lame-duck session that could be a last chance to capitalize on their trifecta.

Between the lines: Republicans decided against breaking for an early recess last week.

  • The biggest thing to show for it: A historic — and bipartisan — college sports package that doesn't do much for those defending their seats in November. It faces long odds in the House.

😖 Otherwise it was a week of pain:

  • Failed votes: A vote addressing Americans' concerns about data centers driving up energy costs failed today, as did another to curb congressional stock trades and enforce voter IDs.
  • A line of attack that backfired: A major hearing with Jack Smith was overshadowed by a failed attempt by Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) to link the special counsel and Atlanta prosecutor Fani Willis.
  • The Trump issue: Republicans have been tiptoeing around whether Trump's unpopularity will hurt the party in November, only for Texas nominee Ken Paxton to be caught blaming Trump's midterm convention for hurting his polling.
  • NRSC Chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) said Paxton's analysis was "just wrong" and called the convention "a boost in the right direction."

🤕 Zoom out: Some of the GOP senators are returning to fresh campaign headaches.

  • Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) lost a week of in-state campaigning and didn't even get a vote on one of her key priorities: a bipartisan bill to lower insulin costs.
  • Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) is the target of a new ad campaign hitting him over his pardon of a man who pleaded guilty to first-degree sexual assault.
  • Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) has been batting down accusations that he went after mothers of new babies over unpaid medical bills. His lawyers sent a cease-and-desist letter to his opponent — Rev. Adam Hamilton — on Monday.

The GOP has a cash advantage, but the campaign apparatus now has to spend heavily in states Trump handily won in 2024 — Ohio, Iowa, Alaska, Texas, Kansas, Nebraska and Florida.

‼️ The other side: Former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) was also hit with a damaging report from the New York Times about her personal behavior and office culture (some of which she denied). She is challenging GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan.

What to watch: The Senate will return in November staring down a list of must-pass items.

  • Fund the government
  • Pass the National Defense Authorization Act
  • Reinstate FISA Section 702, the warrantless wiretap authority
  • Pass the farm bill

💰 The bottom line: That's just what they must get done. There's also a growing list of maybe-to-dos, like:

  • Take a whack at a bipartisan permitting reform bill that finally came together hours before the Senate took off for home.
  • Pass some form of AI guardrails.
  • Raise the debt ceiling, potentially through reconciliation.

item.title: Scoop: Rubio ordered Iranian delegation to leave the country, U.S. official says
item.description:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio demanded on Monday that the Iranian delegation to the United Nations General Assembly immediately leave the country after negotiations stalled, according to a U.S. official and a second source with knowledge of the matter.

Why it matters: Though the Iranians were likely to depart soon anyway, Rubio's move was a highly unusual diplomatic rebuke and laid bare the deep distrust between the two countries amid fruitless efforts to broker an end to the war.

  • Qatari mediators tried to secure a diplomatic breakthrough between the U.S. and Iran but made little progress, with neither side willing to budge.
  • Among those ordered to leave New York was Rubio's Iranian counterpart, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.

What they're saying: "Secretary Rubio kicked out the Iranian delegation who had overstayed their welcome. The UN General Assembly was over, so it was time for them to go," the U.S. official said.

Behind the scenes: On Monday morning, the White House thought there might be progress in talks with Iran later in the day. But by late afternoon it became clear negotiations were at a stalemate.

  • Then on Monday evening, at Rubio's orders, the U.S. mission to the UN told the Iranian mission to the UN that Araghchi's delegation had to leave New York immediately, according to the U.S. official.
  • The Iranian delegation, including Araghchi, left for the airport several hours later and boarded a flight from New York to Doha at 1:20 a.m. Tuesday.
  • A second source confirmed that the U.S. demanded that the Iranian delegation leave, but said Araghchi was scheduled to travel back to Tehran on Monday night anyway.

What's next: Qatari mediators are continuing to talk to both sides about their compromise proposal, regional sources say.

  • "Maybe I will blow 'em up," President Trump told reporters on Wednesday when asked how he can reach a deal with a regime he says is crazy. "Maybe I blow 'em up. We have to make that decision. We will blow 'em up or make a deal. But the time is coming. It's gonna end very soon one way or the other."

item.title: Netanyahu says FlyDubai pilots prevented a "9/11 disaster"
item.description:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu revealed new details about a FlyDubai flight bound for Israel during which a pilot stabbed a colleague, sending the plane spiraling thousands of feet.

The big picture: Netanyahu told CNN Wednesday evening that the Indian pilot who was stabbed, Capt. Smit Machchhar, unlocked the cockpit after being attacked and an Israeli passenger who works as a plumber, Yaniv Hayun, entered and found the Omani pilot apparently trying to interfere with the aircraft's controls.

  • Netanyahu said the suspect was being interrogated in Saudi Arabia and that the UAE agreed Israel could participate in the interrogation.

What they're saying: The Israeli prime minister told CNN's Jim Sciutto that passengers heard shouts and screams coming from the cockpit and that the plumber saw the attacking pilot hovering over the instruments, noting "he was trying to jam the instruments."

  • The plumber pulled back on the aircraft's controls, while another passenger and crew member subdued the attacker, according to Netanyahu. Reserve pilots then came in and stabilized the plane.
  • Netanyahu said he met Hayun at the airport and that the passenger was "drenched" in the Indian pilot's blood.

President Trump said Netanyahu and others had briefed him on what happened.

  • He called the stabbed pilot a "hero" for managing to open the cockpit door and also praised the plumber's actions.

Flashback: Netanyahu noted his own history with hijackings: He was wounded while taking part in the 1972 Israeli commando raid that freed passengers from a hijacked Sabena flight. His brother Yoni was killed four years later while leading the Entebbe hostage rescue.

Reality check: Netanyahu made clear that investigators don't have any specific information that Tehran had anything to do with this incident.

The bottom line: "Those pilots managed to prevent a 9/11 disaster, because that's what it looks like was happening," Netanyahu said.

item.title: AI safety fears put OpenAI and Anthropic in the FTC's crosshairs
item.description:
The Federal Trade Commission is investigating OpenAI, Anthropic and other AI companies over potential safety risks posed by their products, an agency spokesperson told Axios Wednesday.

Why it matters: The federal government has largely taken a hands-off approach to regulating AI, but the FTC investigation could signal a shift for the industry.

Driving the news: FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson is preparing civil investigative demands that would compel AI executives to turn over documents and testify about the safety of their models, according to the New York Post, which first reported the news.

  • The probe has been underway for weeks, predating OpenAI's disclosure that models it was testing escaped their sandbox and compromised parts of AI platform Hugging Face's production infrastructure.
  • OpenAI announced Monday that it would halt the release of its newest model, GPT-6.1 Astra, after it performed poorly on safety testing.

ChatGPT maker OpenAI and Claude maker Anthropic did not respond to Axios' request for comment.

Between the lines: The recent push by top AI executives for increased guardrails around their technology has prompted some AI critics to question their motives.

  • Ferguson recently said that AI firms are trying to panic Americans into pressuring policymakers to build a regulatory "moat" that would allow AI frontrunners to block smaller competitors from catching up.

Catch up quick: News of the ongoing investigation comes just a day after top AI companies sent representatives to the White House to sign a pledge with President Trump to self-police their AI development.

  • Trump compared it to something of a "constitution," but the rules the companies agreed to are similar to what they were already doing.

Zoom out: The new reporting comes shortly after Axios exclusively reported that OpenAI, Anthropic and security researchers were investigating tens of thousands of potential security incidents, including some that had not previously been disclosed to the public.

  • That reporting was later cited Monday when Florida's attorney general asked a court for a temporary injunction against OpenAI, alleging inadequate safety measures.
  • On Tuesday, a public interest law group sued OpenAI over the Hugging Face breach, claiming, among other things, that the company was "knowingly employing an unfair business practice that threatens serious harm on the public."

Go deeper... Scoop: Top AI companies probing tens of thousands of security incidents

Editor's note: Axios' Maria Curi contributed reporting.

item.title: Ask Trump's AI chatbot who won in 2020. You might not get an answer.
item.description:
The Trump administration's new AI service gave users conflicting responses to politically sensitive questions Tuesday and Wednesday: sometimes answering them and sometimes refusing.

The big picture: As the Trump administration increasingly uses AI and answers the public's questions through America.gov, statements carrying the government's authority are shaped by models, instructions and guardrails the public can't see.

  • The White House told Axios in a statement, "America.gov will continue to be updated to provide Americans the most accurate and reliable federal information and resources."
  • America.gov, powered by Google's Gemini and Elon Musk's Grok, aims to help Americans navigate government-related tasks using an AI chatbot — but it quickly drew attention for another reason: It was debunking some of President Trump's long-standing claims.

Driving the news: On Tuesday, Axios — like other outlets — found America.gov contradicted the president on the 2020 election and the Jan. 6 attack.

  • It also confirmed former President Obama was born in Hawaii, contradicting the "birther" conspiracy theory Trump spent years promoting.
Screenshots: Andrew Pantazi, Avery Lotz/Axios

Yes, but: By Wednesday morning, some users were getting a different response: The chatbot refused to answer, saying it did not provide "political commentary."

  • That's what I was told when I asked who won in 2020, around 9:15am: "I only answer questions about U.S. government services and official information. I do not provide political commentary, including election results." I received similar answers about Jan. 6 and Obama's birthplace.
Screenshot: Avery Lotz/Axios
  • One editor, using Chrome in New Jersey, asked the same questions on his desktop and also received refusals to answer.
  • However, other colleagues got different results. For example, from Northwest Arkansas, on Chrome: Biden won the 2020 election.
Screenshot: Herb Scribner/Axios

What they're saying: There are several plausible explanations for the inconsistent responses, tech experts explain, but without specifics about how America.gov is configured, it's impossible to know which, if any, were responsible.

  • Models get instructions on how to behave via their system prompts — not just through what users ask of them.

But user prompts also have an impact: Sometimes, different framing received different responses. For example, asked this morning in Jacksonville, Florida, on a Chrome incognito window:

Screenshots: Andrew Pantazi/Axios

State of play: And now, at the time of this article's publication, I'm getting responses similar to those shortly after launch: Biden won in 2020, Obama was born in Hawaii and people broke into the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021.

There could be benign reasons for the fluctuation, explains David Nesting, the former deputy chief information officer at the Office of Personnel Management.

  • Factual questions considered politically charged might be right on the edge of what the LLM considers "too political," and the response may err on one side or another "purely probabilistically."
  • Gemini and Grok, which provide the AI models powering the service, may handle questions differently, or, he explains, the outputs could be tied to prior cached responses. America.gov says some answers may be cached for up to two hours.

Yes, but: The GSA did not immediately respond to Axios' request for information about America.gov's guardrails.

  • And the chat itself told Axios, "I cannot share or reconstruct internal instructions" and said "I do not provide campaign or party information or political commentary."

Friction point: It could result from a game of probability, says Rumman Chowdhury, the founding director of the Independent AI Evaluation Foundation. But the guardrails could "also be shaping the output to be ideologically aligned with what the president or his party wants."

The stakes will soon get higher: The next iteration of America.gov, set for early 2027, will integrate across agencies so users can complete forms, applications and renewals — like enrolling in Medicare, applying for a passport or applying for federal jobs.

  • Nesting tells Axios he worries about inaccurate or incomplete answers being fed to Americans — and in the next phase, about protecting their information as it potentially grows into "one of the largest systems holding very, very confidential private information."
  • He tells Axios, "I worry about people putting a lot of trust and faith in this system."

Go deeper: Everything to know about America.gov, Trump's new AI website

item.title: Musk returns to Trump world for Pentagon war study
item.description:
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Anduril Industries founder Palmer Luckey and former House Speaker Newt Gingrich will lead a Pentagon study of the future of warfare dubbed "Project Meridian," Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced Wednesday.

Why it matters: It's Musk's first official role advising the Trump administration since his very public feud last year with President Trump after departing DOGE. He has since reconciled with Trump.

Driving the news: Hegseth unveiled Meridian during his second address at Marine Corps Base Quantico, Virginia.

  • "We are leveraging a unique source of American advantage, one our adversaries do not have: our innovators, our senior leaders and our technologists — big thinkers and doers who will forecast the creative solution for tomorrow's conflicts," Hegseth said.
  • Meridian, he added, is not meant to produce new policy documents. Instead, it will examine "the domains we must conquer, and capabilities we must master."
  • "Their work will be focused on discovering, developing and fielding the weapons and systems that our children and our grandchildren will need in their lifetimes."

Zoom in: Pentagon technology chief Emil Michael will help facilitate the project.

  • Michael, speaking to reporters in December about America's industrial base, said he would like to see "five more Andurils and Palantirs and SpaceXs" flourish.

What they're saying: "Americans have always been at our best when we bring our smartest scientists, engineers and technologists together to solve the hardest problems in national security," Luckey told Axios.

  • "Together, we will not only study the wars being fought today but also think seriously about the wars we cannot afford to fight in 2030, 2050, and 2100 — and what America needs to build now to prevent them."

Follow the money: Musk's and Luckey's respective companies have big Pentagon contracts.

  • SpaceX serves as America's national-security launch backbone, while Anduril furnishes jammers, interceptors, rocket motors and robo-wingmen.

What's next: The Meridian leadership was expected to meet for the first time on Wednesday. Final findings are expected in 120 days, Hegseth said.

  • A public rollout is planned, along with a classified report.

Go deeper: Hegseth to generals: Embrace MAGA military or quit

item.title: Fed watchdog clears former chair Powell in renovation probe
item.description:
A Federal Reserve watchdog found no criminal wrongdoing by former chair Jerome Powell in its investigation of the central bank's expensive headquarters renovation, according to a report released on Wednesday.

Why it matters: The findings effectively clear Powell after the Justice Department opened an unprecedented criminal investigation into then-Fed chair, which became public in January.

What they're saying: "At no point during our evaluation did we find reasonable grounds to believe that a violation of federal criminal law had occurred requiring a referral to the U.S. Attorney General," the Office of Inspector General wrote in the report.

  • The watchdog added that it "did not identify administrative misconduct during our evaluation."

Yes, but: While the report clears Powell, it faults Fed management and oversight of the project as construction costs more than doubled to $2.5 billion.

  • The Fed "did not take numerous actions available to it that could have better controlled costs and mitigated some of the significant construction cost increases," the report says.

Flashback: The renovation became a flashpoint in President Trump's broader campaign against Powell and the Fed.

  • Trump toured the construction site with Powell in July 2025 and publicly challenged him over the project's soaring costs.

Zoom out: The Justice Department's investigation centered on Powell's June 2025 testimony to Congress about the renovation and its rising costs.

  • Powell denied wrongdoing and argued at the time that the investigation was part of a broader effort to pressure the Fed over interest rates.
  • DOJ closed the investigation in April as the Fed's inspector general continued its review.

Zoom in: The watchdog said that inflation alone could not explain the project's higher costs.

  • For instance, the report shows that two major mechanical, electrical and plumbing contracts more than tripled to $539 million from an earlier $178 million estimate, far outpacing the broader rise in construction costs.

Of note: The report says that the key design features that drew scrutiny from Congress and other critics — including marble, water features and a garden terrace — did not materially contribute to the project's cost increases.

  • The Fed removed four planned new fountains in June 2025 because officials worried about "external stakeholders, such as Congress and the media, raising concerns about the design," according to the report.

What to watch: Powell has remained on the Fed's board after his term as chair ended in May — an unusual move that he said was tied to seeing the investigation through to its conclusion.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.
item.content:encoded:
A Federal Reserve watchdog found no criminal wrongdoing by former chair Jerome Powell in its investigation of the central bank's expensive headquarters renovation, according to a report released on Wednesday.

Why it matters: The findings effectively clear Powell after the Justice Department opened an unprecedented criminal investigation into then-Fed chair, which became public in January.

What they're saying: "At no point during our evaluation did we find reasonable grounds to believe that a violation of federal criminal law had occurred requiring a referral to the U.S. Attorney General," the Office of Inspector General wrote in the report.

  • The watchdog added that it "did not identify administrative misconduct during our evaluation."

Yes, but: While the report clears Powell, it faults Fed management and oversight of the project as construction costs more than doubled to $2.5 billion.

  • The Fed "did not take numerous actions available to it that could have better controlled costs and mitigated some of the significant construction cost increases," the report says.

Flashback: The renovation became a flashpoint in President Trump's broader campaign against Powell and the Fed.

  • Trump toured the construction site with Powell in July 2025 and publicly challenged him over the project's soaring costs.

Zoom out: The Justice Department's investigation centered on Powell's June 2025 testimony to Congress about the renovation and its rising costs.

  • Powell denied wrongdoing and argued at the time that the investigation was part of a broader effort to pressure the Fed over interest rates.
  • DOJ closed the investigation in April as the Fed's inspector general continued its review.

Zoom in: The watchdog said that inflation alone could not explain the project's higher costs.

  • For instance, the report shows that two major mechanical, electrical and plumbing contracts more than tripled to $539 million from an earlier $178 million estimate, far outpacing the broader rise in construction costs.

Of note: The report says that the key design features that drew scrutiny from Congress and other critics — including marble, water features and a garden terrace — did not materially contribute to the project's cost increases.

  • The Fed removed four planned new fountains in June 2025 because officials worried about "external stakeholders, such as Congress and the media, raising concerns about the design," according to the report.

What to watch: Powell has remained on the Fed's board after his term as chair ended in May — an unusual move that he said was tied to seeing the investigation through to its conclusion.

item.title: Google unveils long-awaited Gemini 4
item.description:
Google is unveiling its long-awaited next-generation AI model, Gemini 4 Argon, to a small group of cybersecurity partners, the company said Wednesday.

Why it matters: Gemini 4 arrives after a long gap at the top of Google's model lineup, in which the company kept rolling out smaller, cheaper Flash models while rivals OpenAI and Anthropic sprinted forward.

State of play: Google says Gemini 4 Argon is built to handle complex, long-running tasks in software engineering, finance, legal work and cybersecurity.

  • Google said the new model is state of the art on certain coding and knowledge work benchmarks, outperforming competing OpenAI frontier model GPT-6 Astra on several.
  • The company is rolling the model out only to a group of trusted cybersecurity defenders and is participating in the U.S. government's voluntary pre-release process.
  • Google says it will expand access after additional testing, with paying subscribers first in line.

What they're saying: "Argon is a well-rounded model that has frontier capabilities across several domains," Tulsee Doshi, head of Gemini products at Google DeepMind, told Axios.

  • "We've seen strong performance up close as Googlers have put the model through its paces in recent weeks, with many relying on it for their hardest coding and research problems."

Flashback: Gemini 4 comes out nearly a year after the previous flagship model generation, Gemini 3.

  • In May, Google CEO Sundar Pichai said the company's next major model release would come in June.
  • That model, widely expected to be Gemini 3.5 Pro, never came out.
  • In July, Axios reported that poor morale among Google DeepMind employees was part of the reason for the delay.

Zoom in: Google's additional time investment may not be viewed as negatively in the context of the AI safety debate that has embroiled companies and users.

  • OpenAI has had issues with agents going rogue, and recently said it is scrapping GPT-6.1 Astra due to security issues.
  • Top AI developers OpenAI and Anthropic are investigating tens of thousands of incidents involving their agents misbehaving, Axios previously reported.

The bottom line: If the developer community finds Gemini 4 to be as competitive with OpenAI and Anthropic's frontier systems as the benchmarks indicate, it would result in a massive catch-up for an AI company some had started to doubt.

item.title: Trump's DOJ takes its fight with federal judges to Minnesota
item.description:
The Justice Department filed a complaint against a group of federal judges from Minnesota for speaking to The New York Times about the impact of the immigration enforcement surge on their court.

The big picture: The complaint opens a new front in the Trump administration's standoff with federal judges, bolstered by a loyal Justice Department.

Driving the news: The complaint, which was brought against two jurists who spoke on the record with the paper and those who spoke anonymously, alleged the behavior was "improper and unethical" and called for the judges to be recused from any DHS-related matters.

  • It further urged the Eighth Circuit to investigate.
  • The chambers of the named senior district judges, Patrick J. Schiltz and John R. Tunheim, did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment.

This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

item.title: Hegseth accuses media of treason in pugnacious annual address
item.description:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth took aim at the U.S. media during a speech at a Marine Corps base in Virginia on Wednesday, saying: "Our so-called press makes Iranian state media look reasonable."

Why it matters: Hegseth cast news outlets as a threat to U.S. troops, escalating his attacks on journalists over reporting based on classified information.

What he's saying: In his second annual "State of the Force" address at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia, Hegseth accused some members of the media of "treason."

  • While a free press is important, he said "partisan activism that intentionally smears the troops and the historic mission that they're undertaking is fundamentally anti-American. It's sick. It's a national betrayal. It's treason, actually."
  • "It's your movements and bases that they reveal to the enemy," he said. "Ultimately, it's your lives they put directly at risk when they lie about munition stockpiles."

Between the lines: Media reports about dwindling supplies of key munitions amid the war with Iran have drawn the ire of President Trump and his team. Hegseth frequently attacks the press and has taken unprecedented steps to restrict the media's access to the Pentagon.

Driving the news: Hegseth returned to many culture-war themes in the speech, highlighting his efforts to reverse DEI and gender equity efforts in the interest of "meritocracy."

  • "We are no longer the woke department or the weak department. Simple translation of that — no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors."

Zoom out: Hegseth also made substantive news in the speech. He confirmed plans for a 20% reduction in generals and admirals across the force, while rejecting descriptions of the cuts as a purge.

  • "As usual, what the media levels as an accusation, I wear as an accomplishment," he said.
  • Hegseth also announced a new Autonomous Warfare Command, an initiative to study the future of war that will involve Elon Musk, and a nationwide competition to host the next U.S. military base.

Go deeper: Hegseth directs Pentagon to combat foreign interference in U.S. elections

item.title: Exclusive: HHS launches project to speed up clinical trials
item.description:
The Trump administration on Wednesday is launching an effort to reimagine the way clinical trials are designed, with a goal of drastically reducing the time and money it takes to develop new drugs.

Why it matters: The program, shared first with Axios, could provide a template for reconfiguring the drug development process and boosting U.S. competitiveness in the global biotech race.

Driving the news: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. and Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health Director Alicia Jackson are unveiling the new effort in Austin, Texas.

  • CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz and FDA Acting Commissioner Kyle Diamantas will also attend the announcement.
  • The effort — dubbed the Simulation-augmented, Real-time Platform Adaptive Seamless Trials (SURPASS) program — features teams selected through a bidding process that will bring drug candidates through experimental clinical trial processes.

How it works: The initiative under ARPA-H will begin by soliciting ideas from "teams" that include a drug sponsor. Winners will receive funding and support over five years.

  • ARPA-H is looking for proposals that innovate in three technical areas: Phaseless trials that allow faster trials with fewer patients, the ability to analyze data in real time during the trial instead of than only when it ends, and using automation to reduce inefficiencies.
  • Teams will also likely include medical centers or other clinical sites, biostatisticians, and companies that have the ability to predict drug outcomes via a computer.
  • The FDA has been included in the planning of the program, and "there won't be any surprises for regulators in this," said Daria Fedyukina, the program manager.

The big picture: One of the reasons China has become such a popular location for drug manufacturers is because it's much cheaper and faster to do early-stage clinical trials there.

  • Experts and the biopharmaceutical community largely agree that in order to compete, the U.S. needs to streamline its trial processes.
  • Today, developing a drug can take longer than a decade and cost around $2 billion. More than 90% of drug candidates fail, according to HHS.

What they're saying: "The goal is to develop the tech that is missing and blaze the trail of a new clinical trial paradigm," Fedyukina said.

  • The program will require the development of "blueprints and standards that then can be deployed and used by all other trials in the U.S," she added.
  • While "it's hard to put a number to how much cost savings or time savings we can achieve," Fedyukina said, "there is no reason why we cannot target, let's say, a 10x reduction in the cost of clinical development for a drug."
  • "There's no reason why we cannot cut timeline in half or more," she added.

Details: ARPA-H is also announcing three related projects today aimed at improving the infrastructure around clinical trials.

  • One is focused on setting up more clinical trial sites, with the help of AI to speed up site activation and prepare sites that haven't held trials before.
  • This will allow patients who live near hospitals that don't currently participate in clinical trials to gain access to experimental drugs they may benefit from.
  • The other two projects focus on clinical trial data infrastructure and helping patients with complex cancers benefit from their own data and better navigate the care system.

The bottom line: This is all an experiment, but if successful it could pay big dividends.

item.title: Jack Smith faces new lawsuit over congressional phone records
item.description:
Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) sued former special counsel Jack Smith Wednesday, alleging he unlawfully obtained her cellphone toll records during his investigation of Trump and the 2020 election

Why it matters: The lawsuit escalates Republicans' efforts to challenge Smith's investigation more than a year after his probe ended.

What they're saying: "Through his Arctic Frost witch hunt that targeted conservatives across America and even the President of the United States, Jack Smith perpetrated one of the worst abuses of government power in our nation's history," Blackburn said.

  • "This lawsuit is solely about holding Mr. Smith accountable and ensuring that our nation's justice system can never again be weaponized against the American people. I thank the New Civil Liberties Alliance for their partnership in filing this complaint and for fighting to uphold our cherished constitutional rights."

Driving the news: The suit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee one day after Smith testified at a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing Tuesday.

  • The suit alleges Smith obtained a nondisclosure order without telling the judge that the underlying subpoena sought the records of a sitting senator. Blackburn's cellphone provider was ordered to keep the subpoena secret.
  • Blackburn is asking the court to award her $1 in nominal damages to emphasize that she isn't seeking money but instead wants to hold Smith accountable for his allegedly unlawful actions.
  • Legal counsel for Smith did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment.

Flashback: The lawsuit comes one day after Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.), a potential running mate for JD Vance in 2028, accused Smith of perjury at Tuesday's hearing but got his facts wrong and was later corrected by Smith and Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.).

  • The mistake went viral and drew extensive criticism on social media.

Catch up quick: In October 2025, the GOP-led House Judiciary Committee released highly redacted documents showing that the FBI had investigated approximately 160 Republican figures as part of its probe into Trump's false claims that the 2020 presidential election was stolen.

  • The probe, known as Arctic Frost, sought to identify those who "conspired to corruptly obstruct the United States Congress' certification of the 2020 Presidential election results by submitting allegedly fraudulent elector certificates."

By the numbers: The lawsuit claims the Arctic Frost probe subpoenaed records associated with at least 20 Republican members of Congress.

  • The lawsuit claims about 400 Republican individuals and organizations were targeted.
  • The lawsuit says records involving roughly 4,782 Trump donors, including 102 Tennesseans, contained home addresses, bank account numbers and signatures.

The bottom line: Blackburn's lawsuit extends the legal and political fight over the Justice Department's investigations into Trump after he left office.

  • Trump and his allies have vowed to continue probing those who investigated or crossed the president, including New York Attorney General Letitia James (D), former FBI chief James Comey and Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.).

Go deeper: Jan. 6 probe potentially investigated over 150 Republicans, documents show

item.title: 944 children abused by Catholic clergy, Mass. AG says — but no new charges
item.description:
The Massachusetts attorney general released a report Wednesday documenting more than 270 Catholic clerics accused of sexually abusing 944 children across three dioceses — but the investigation will result in no new indictments.

Why it matters: The dioceses created an illusion of safety while church leaders repeatedly exploited loopholes to protect the institution's reputation, systematically concealing staggering levels of abuse.

What they're saying: "We deeply understand that behind every number is a child whose safety was violated, a family that was changed, and a survivor who has carried the trauma of that abuse for years, and in many cases, decades," Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell (D) wrote in the report.

Catch up quick: The Massachusetts AG's office began its investigation in 2019, examining church responses to abuse allegations over more than six decades.

  • Boston Globe reporters exposed widespread abuse and institutional cover-ups in the Archdiocese of Boston in the early 2000s.
  • Wednesday's report sought to provide the first comparable public accounting of what happened in the Roman Catholic dioceses of Fall River, Springfield and Worcester.
  • Investigators reviewed more than 300,000 pages of documents and interviewed more than 100 people, including survivors, attorneys and clergy.

Worth noting: After reporters uncovered the abuse, Massachusetts lawmakers criminalized the reckless endangerment of children and expanded mandated reporter requirements to include clergy.

  • But those laws can't be applied retroactively to crimes that occurred before they took effect.
  • Most of the abuse detailed in the report occurred before 2002, and the AG says newly found misconduct fell outside applicable statutes of limitations. Many accused clergy are also dead, leaving survivors with few options for legal recourse.

Zoom in: The report concluded that diocesan leaders actively covered up abuse allegations before 2002 by transferring accused clergy to new congregations without warning parishioners.

  • Leaders also sent accused priests to psychiatric treatment facilities before allowing some to return to ministry. Some of these priests were then accused of reoffending.

Between the lines: Survivors described church processes that left some feeling pressured to testify to internal church investigators or stay silent and say the dioceses used NDAs to stop survivors from discussing abuse allegations.

  • One survivor recalled a staff member saying, "[t]he best way for this to go away is not to talk about it." The survivor said the church's internal investigator "was as curious to get my story as she was to protect his."
  • Another said an internal review board resembled "a tribunal," adding: "The Church is like your mother: when they call, you answer."
  • Survivor Phil Saviano told the Globe that he had came forward and refused to sign an NDA because he was "dying of AIDS … at that point my career was over, I was on my way out physically, my reputation was shot in the eyes of many people, and I didn't have a lot to lose."

Zoom out: The institutional secrecy that enabled decades of abuse has not been fully addressed: 12 dioceses across the United States still have not published lists of credibly accused clergy.

  • That represents less than 5% of all dioceses and orders. In Massachusetts, Worcester is the only diocese that still has not published a list. The Vatican did not respond to Axios' request for comment.
  • The report says the lists can encourage survivors to come forward, reveal the scope of the abuse and promote transparency and accountability.

A spokesperson for the Worcester Diocese didn't address Axios' question on why they haven't published a list of accused clergy, but said that they "welcome the AG's report."

  • "Our procedures over the past three decades, including the way we screen candidates for ordination, as well as the awareness and safety training which was implemented in all our parishes and ministries, have made an enormous difference," they said.
  • "The diocese has passed each year's independent compliance audit" since a new Charter was adopted in 2002. The charter now "serve[s] as a model for other institutions, public or private, who care for children and minors."

The bottom line: The investigation provides a historical reckoning for nearly 1,000 survivors, but decades of concealment left hundreds with validation and little legal recourse.

Go deeper: Vatican criminalizes sexual abuse of adults by priests

  • One survivor recalled a staff member saying, "[t]he best way for this to go away is not to talk about it." The survivor said the church's internal investigator "was as curious to get my story as she was to protect his."
  • Another said an internal review board resembled "a tribunal," adding: "The Church is like your mother: when they call, you answer."
  • Survivor Phil Saviano told the Globe that he had came forward and refused to sign an NDA because he was "dying of AIDS … at that point my career was over, I was on my way out physically, my reputation was shot in the eyes of many people, and I didn't have a lot to lose."

Zoom out: The institutional secrecy that enabled decades of abuse has not been fully addressed: 12 dioceses across the United States still have not published lists of credibly accused clergy.

  • That represents less than 5% of all dioceses and orders. In Massachusetts, Worcester is the only diocese that still has not published a list. The Vatican did not respond to Axios' request for comment.
  • The report says the lists can encourage survivors to come forward, reveal the scope of the abuse and promote transparency and accountability.

A spokesperson for the Worcester Diocese didn't address Axios' question on why they haven't published a list of accused clergy, but said that they "welcome the AG's report."

  • "Our procedures over the past three decades, including the way we screen candidates for ordination, as well as the awareness and safety training which was implemented in all our parishes and ministries, have made an enormous difference," they said.
  • "The diocese has passed each year's independent compliance audit" since a new Charter was adopted in 2002. The charter now "serve[s] as a model for other institutions, public or private, who care for children and minors."

The bottom line: The investigation provides a historical reckoning for nearly 1,000 survivors, but decades of concealment left hundreds with validation and little legal recourse.

Go deeper: Vatican criminalizes sexual abuse of adults by priests

item.title: "Strong indications" Iran had role in U.K. bomb plot, PM Andy Burnham says
item.description:
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there are "strong indications that Iran played a part" in a suspected bomb plot at a British air base used by the U.S.

The big picture: Burnham's comments to the BBC come after Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that the weekend incident at RAF Fairford "clearly involves the hands ‌of a foreign actor." Tehran denies any involvement.

  • Five British men were released on bail Monday following their arrest a day earlier in connection with the alleged plot.

What they're saying: "We will say more in due course but we can confirm ... that we believe Iran to have played a part," Burnham told the BBC, declining to elaborate.

  • He emphasized that the counter-terrorism investigation is ongoing and "complex" and that investigators are "working closely with our colleagues" in the U.S.
  • Rubio told Fox News Monday that the incident "ties us to the reality here, and that is we are dealing with elements in the world — and in the case of Iran, for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally."

Context: U.K. earlier this year allowed the U.S. Air Force to use RAF Fairford for limited defensive strikes against Iranian missile capabilities.

  • Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps named RAF Fairford in July when it said that any British base used for attacks on Iranian territory would be considered a "legitimate target."

item.title: Exclusive: Cornell rape allegations fuel House Democratic women's Title IX push
item.description:
A criminal investigation into allegations that a Cornell University student was gang raped by seven fraternity members in 2024 is fueling a new push by House Democratic women to strengthen federal protections against sexual violence on college campuses.

Why it matters: The Democratic Women's Caucus is calling on congressional Republicans and the Trump administration to strengthen Title IX protections, arguing that the administration's changes to the civil rights law could leave students more vulnerable.

  • The push comes just two days after the Trump administration rescinded Biden-era sex discrimination Title IX regulations and reinstated rules adopted during President Trump's first term.
  • The Democratic Women's Caucus argues those changes have "eroded the processes in place for sexual misconduct investigations."

Driving the news: "Her story should be a wake-up call Republicans cannot ignore: we need stronger protections and systems for survivors, and we need to act now," Democratic Women's Caucus Chair Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.) and Vice Chairs Emilia Sykes (D-Ohio) and Hillary Scholten (D-Mich.) said in a statement first shared with Axios.

  • The lawmakers argue the Cornell case underscores the need for stronger federal protections and more aggressive enforcement of Title IX, the landmark law barring sex discrimination at federally funded schools that also governs how schools respond to sexual harassment and assault allegations.
  • They called on the administration and Republicans to "condemn what took place at Cornell, stand in solidarity with Jane Doe, and work with us to better protect survivors and ensure they can seek justice."

Catch up quick: A former Cornell University student, referred to as "Jane Doe" in legal documents, is suing the school, seven Chi Phi fraternity members and others over allegations that she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house in October of 2024.

  • Cornell conducted a Title IX investigation after "Jane Doe" reported the incident in 2024 that resulted in two of the students being expelled and lesser disciplinary action for the other students.
  • The DA has said criminal charges were not pursued because Jane Doe's initial police statement did not allege that she was gang-raped or drugged against her will.

A criminal investigation was reopened after the lawsuit was filed earlier this month, and the New York attorney general has launched a separate review of the university's handling of the allegations. No criminal charges have been filed.

  • The lack of criminal charges and the university's handling of the alleged incident have has sparked intense scrutiny over how colleges respond to sexual assault.
  • Cornell said in a statement last week that the university "investigated and adjudicated the allegations consistent with university policies," and said in a statement this week that the university supports the DA's decision to reopen the criminal case. Cornell did not respond to a request for comment from Axios.

Zoom out: The latest Title IX fight in Washington has largely centered on sexual orientation and gender identity, but also impacts how colleges handle sexual misconduct allegations.

  • The Biden administration broadened the definition of sex-based harassment covered by Title IX and gave colleges more flexibility in investigating sexual misconduct.
  • Trump returned to his first-term rules, which narrow the definition of sexual harassment, require more formal proceedings for handling misconduct allegations, and give schools more flexibility in deciding how much evidence is needed to discipline a student.
  • Democrats argue those requirements create additional hurdles for survivors seeking protection under Title IX.

What we're watching: Whether the Cornell allegations generate bipartisan interest in strengthening federal campus sexual assault protections.

item.title: SCOTUS says Tennessee can move forward with Christa Pike's execution
item.description:
The U.S. Supreme Court said Wednesday night that Tennessee could move forward with death row inmate Christa Pike's execution, reversing a last-minute stay issued earlier in the day by a federal appeals court.

The latest: The high court cleared the way for the execution in a two-sentence order that capped a rapid-fire legal battle. The three liberal justices dissented.

  • It wasn't immediately clear when the state would move forward with the execution, which was initially set to take place Wednesday morning.

Catch up quick: The 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals had ordered "a short stay of execution" so it could consider an ongoing legal battle between Pike's attorneys and the state.

  • The last-minute appeals court order came in about an hour before Pike's scheduled lethal injection at 10am in Nashville.
  • Two members of a three-judge appeals panel backed the stay. The third judge disagreed, describing Pike's legal fight as a "last-ditch meritless effort to delay a lawful execution."
  • The Tennessee attorney general's office quickly asked the U.S. Supreme Court to intervene and allow the execution to proceed.

Between the lines: Pike's attorneys argue her history of child sexual abuse wasn't presented to the jury before she was sentenced to death in 1996.

Zoom in: Pike, the only woman on Tennessee's death row, was convicted and sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, who was beaten to death. Pike was 18 at the time.

  • Two other people were convicted in the case, but only Pike got the death penalty.
  • Pike's advocates do not contest her guilt, but they argue that her history of childhood abuse should have been presented to the jury during the sentencing phase as "important context and mitigation for the offense."

Editor's note: This story was updated with the latest news that the U.S. Supreme Court has vacated the appeals court's stay.

item.title: Trump's AI "constitution" crowns day of accelerating ambition
item.description:
With America's tech titans crowded around a single White House table Tuesday, President Trump extracted what he called a "morally binding" compact on AI safety.

  • The terms were simple: Press ahead, project optimism and police yourselves.

Why it matters: The White House Accord on Super Intelligence, signed by OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, xAI and Nvidia, formalizes industry self-regulation as Washington's response to the most alarming run of AI safety failures yet.

Zoom in: Trump, who increasingly treats American AI dominance as central to his legacy, cast the accord as proof that an industry fractured over safety can still govern itself.

  • He compared the document to "a constitution," claimed there was "a lot of commonality" among the tech leaders, and praised what he described as "tremendous self-policing."
  • The one-page pact, which is deliberately light-touch, calls for "four layers of controls and auditing," including outside evaluators and independent board oversight.

Between the lines: The accord makes a vague reference to future "laws or regulations," preserving the possibility of a tougher federal regime if ultimately needed.

  • Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, a MAGA bogeyman and the industry's most prominent advocate for slowing frontier development, signed the pact but stressed to reporters that it was only "a start."
  • Trump AI adviser David Sacks, by contrast, treated the accord as mission accomplished — declaring on X that the companies were "accepting responsibility" for AI safety thanks to Trump's leadership.

Zoom out: The White House pact capped an extraordinary day for the AI race across three capitals of American power.

1. In Washington, Trump spent Tuesday pulling AI deeper into both the machinery and mythology of his presidency.

  • In the morning, he unveiled America.gov, an AI-powered front door to federal services, and vowed not to "stifle" a technology he says will eclipse the Industrial Revolution.
  • Hours later, Trump signed an executive order directing the federal government to replace "AI" with "Super Intelligence" in official usage — and called on Congress to write the new terminology into law.

2. In Silicon Valley, OpenAI spent the day racing deeper into the age of autonomous AI while struggling to contain its risks.

  • At its highly anticipated DevDay, the company unveiled a sweeping slate of products designed to make AI more persistent, capable and independent in everyday life, including a new personal assistant.
  • But midway through Sam Altman's keynote, an explosive New York Times report revealed that OpenAI executives had brushed aside internal safety warnings months before its models began hacking outside systems.

3. On Wall Street, Anthropic's leaked IPO prospectus distilled the surreal economics of the AI race.

  • According to Reuters, the company laid out a path to a valuation north of $2 trillion while warning prospective investors that its technology could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity."
  • Altman, meanwhile, said OpenAI would delay its own IPO until it could "make confident safety decisions" — even as the company reportedly seeks at least $30 billion in private funding at a roughly $1.4 trillion valuation.

The bottom line: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, seated beside Trump at the White House, supplied the day's credo: "Trust and innovation are not in conflict. Safety is how trust is earned."

item.title: AI agents have a normal-people problem
item.description:
AI companies are staking their future on the mass adoption of agents, hoping that they can solve the annoyances of modern life — email, travel bookings, online purchases.

Why it matters: The frenzy around Meta's Muse shows there's serious consumer curiosity about the technology. But most Americans live life beyond a computer screen and find much of their meaning outside of the 9-5.

  • There's little evidence that they're willing to invest the time needed to re-engineer their lives in a way that puts AI at the center.
  • And the more worrying issue for AI companies: What happens if people just don't want an assistant that leads them to do more work or allows them to be more productive?

Driving the news: Muse vaulted to the top of Apple's App Store on the back of its integrations with Facebook and Instagram and a cute, fuzzy mascot. Meta expanded it to business customers, too. Muse's early success has given the industry hope that there's potential for the tech to break through.

  • Meta isn't alone. Microsoft released a souped-up Copilot with an agentic Autopilot feature, folding more advanced AI into the workplace. And OpenAI announced its own agentic assistant, dots, this week.

The big roadblock is that most Americans don't use AI chatbots, let alone agents.

  • Back in February, Pew found that 51% avoided using AI chatbots entirely. Of those people, 79% who didn't use chatbots cited privacy concerns and 67% were unlikely to use a chatbot in the next year.

The even bigger problem: Agents only become truly useful when people hand them access to their digital lives — and people really don't want to.

  • A huge international Thales poll this year found broad pushback against the core uses of agents — only 13% of respondents would let an "AI helper" read their emails, 11% would let one rebook travel and just 7% would let it move money between bank accounts.
  • Even shopping is a no-go: 56% told YouGov they wouldn't let an agent shop for them at all. Only 10% trust one with more than $25 without approval.

That means the people embracing AI agents right now probably look a lot like the people building them.

  • Menlo Ventures, working with Morning Consult, found that households with incomes over $100,000 are substantially more likely to use AI than households making less than $50,000.
  • People who pay for AI are twice as likely to use it daily — and people who pay for it are five times more likely to use agents.
  • Menlo sums up AI's power spenders this way: "a millennial parent with a post-grad degree working in technology or financial services" who "[tends] to have more money than time."

It'd be wrong to pretend that AI use isn't happening at all. The St. Louis Fed pegs AI adoption as "widespread but shallow" — at least 20% of workers use AI in more than 80% of occupations.

  • But that's heavily weighted toward the same white-collar, tech-adjacent jobs. Adoption for computer programmers, PR people, financial advisors and CEOs all clock around or above 80%. Licensed practical nurses, receptionists and animal caretakers land just at or less than 10%.
  • The St. Louis fed sums it up this way: "Currently, AI works on screens and cannot drive a truck or draw blood."

Between the lines: The frontier labs' own user data shows the same skew.

  • Anthropic found that the two massively overindexed professions in its Economic Index Survey — which the company says isn't representative — were computer/math-related (30% of respondents, 4% of U.S. employment) and management (23% of respondents, 7% of U.S. employment).

The big picture: Only 6% of Americans think that utilizing AI tools like ChatGPT is a very important ingredient for a good life, per Gallup.

  • Compare that to: spending time with a partner, friends or family (78%), exercising or other physical activity (58%), cooking (49%), spending time in nature (45%) or practicing spirituality (42%).

The bottom line: Agentic AI might well be transformative someday — but, for right now, it seems like it'll most impact people who have used the phrase "inbox triage" and feel overwhelmed by Google Calendar notifications.

🎓 Go deeper ... AI 101: Explaining AI to anyone

item.title: Renewables boom faces a Trump-era cliff
item.description:
America is adding record amounts of clean power despite President Trump's opposition to wind and solar — but the industry's top trade group warns the growth could fall off a "cliff" as soon as 2028.

Why it matters: The disconnect illustrates the long lag between energy policy and what actually gets built, raising the stakes for a bipartisan permitting deal under negotiation now in the Senate.

State of play: Wind and solar development is still benefiting from favorable economics and projects launched before Trump returned to the White House, Jason Grumet, CEO of the American Clean Power Association, told Axios.

  • "If the administration continues to block the permitting of clean power, you'll start to see a cliff," said Grumet, who said the drop could become apparent in 2028 or 2029.

Driving the news: Senate negotiators are expected to unveil a bipartisan deal to speed energy permitting as soon as Wednesday, though any final vote isn't expected until after the midterm elections.

Between the lines: Democrats have sought assurances that the administration would allow stalled wind and solar projects to advance in exchange for supporting broader permitting changes.

  • Grumet called the apparent agreement "encouraging," citing its technology-neutral approach and provisions for administration approval of wind projects.
  • "Passage before the end of the year is essential," he said.

By the numbers: Wind and solar account for nearly two-thirds of the new power capacity developers plan to add to the U.S. grid this year, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

  • The first half of 2026 was a record for new wind, solar and battery capacity, Grumet's group reported earlier this month.

The White House says those numbers reflect policies Trump has already changed.

  • When presented with the EIA figures at an Axios event last week, Jarrod Agen, executive director of the White House National Energy Dominance Council, said: "That's a carryover from the policies of the past."
  • The Republican tax-and-spending law Trump signed in July 2025 accelerated the expiration of federal tax credits for new wind and solar projects. Projects generally must begin construction by July 4 of this year, or must come online before 2028 to qualify.

Reality check: Lazard, the financial advisory firm whose analysis is widely used to compare power-generation costs, concluded this year that renewables remain the cheapest forms of new power generation on an unsubsidized basis, although the analysis doesn't capture inherent variability of wind and solar.

  • "We feel that we're on very firm ground in an honest, competitive marketplace, but no industry can overcome active obstruction," Grumet said.

The big picture: The fight is unfolding as U.S. electricity demand rises rapidly, driven largely by the AI boom. That's a contradiction Grumet sees at the heart of Trump's energy policy.

  • "The imperative to repudiate renewables is a greater incentive than the imperative to lower energy costs," he said, calling that "outrageous."

The other side: "The issue the president has with wind and solar is, is it's not going to be the solution for the power needs that we have," Agen said, highlighting nuclear power instead.

  • He rejected the premise that the administration categorically opposes renewable energy, saying they shouldn't have received preferential subsidies and citing dependence on China for energy equipment.
  • A White House official said Tuesday night the administration and lawmakers had agreed to a "strong bipartisan" package, but warned that administration commitments "will not remain frozen indefinitely" if the deal doesn't advance quickly.

Zoom in: Pentagon delays in reviewing onshore wind projects are a key sticking point in the permitting debate.

  • "Just rubber-stamping every project to come in is not good," Agen said.
  • Grumet countered that legitimate military concerns can be addressed: "These are solvable problems."

After Congress accelerated the wind and solar tax credits' expiration last year, Grumet said the industry expected "some return to normalcy."

  • Instead, agencies took what ACP counts as at least 17 actions restricting development, including halting offshore wind leasing, adding political reviews to permits and delaying Pentagon reviews of onshore wind projects.

Catch up quick: Federal courts have blocked several of these moves, including the broad freeze on wind approvals, barriers to renewable permitting and Pentagon reviews.

What we're watching: Trump issued an executive order in August that could restrict certain electrical equipment with ties to China.

  • Depending on how broadly the Energy Department interprets it, Grumet said, "it has the potential to be devastating to the economy."

What's next: The Senate permitting deal could be a bright spot for all energy types, including renewable energy, but final passage is far from guaranteed.
item.content:encoded:
America is adding record amounts of clean power despite President Trump's opposition to wind and solar — but the industry's top trade group warns the growth could fall off a "cliff" as soon as 2028.

Why it matters: The disconnect illustrates the long lag between energy policy and what actually gets built, raising the stakes for a bipartisan permitting deal under negotiation now in the Senate.

State of play: Wind and solar development is still benefiting from favorable economics and projects launched before Trump returned to the White House, Jason Grumet, CEO of the American Clean Power Association, told Axios.

  • "If the administration continues to block the permitting of clean power, you'll start to see a cliff," said Grumet, who said the drop could become apparent in 2028 or 2029.

Driving the news: Senate negotiators are expected to unveil a bipartisan deal to speed energy permitting as soon as Wednesday, though any final vote isn't expected until after the midterm elections.

Between the lines: Democrats have sought assurances that the administration would allow stalled wind and solar projects to advance in exchange for supporting broader permitting changes.

  • Grumet called the apparent agreement "encouraging," citing its technology-neutral approach and provisions for administration approval of wind projects.
  • "Passage before the end of the year is essential," he said.

By the numbers: Wind and solar account for nearly two-thirds of the new power capacity developers plan to add to the U.S. grid this year, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

  • The first half of 2026 was a record for new wind, solar and battery capacity, Grumet's group reported earlier this month.

The White House says those numbers reflect policies Trump has already changed.

  • When presented with the EIA figures at an Axios event last week, Jarrod Agen, executive director of the White House National Energy Dominance Council, said: "That's a carryover from the policies of the past."
  • The Republican tax-and-spending law Trump signed in July 2025 accelerated the expiration of federal tax credits for new wind and solar projects. Projects generally must begin construction by July 4 of this year, or must come online before 2028 to qualify.

Reality check: Lazard, the financial advisory firm whose analysis is widely used to compare power-generation costs, concluded this year that renewables remain the cheapest forms of new power generation on an unsubsidized basis, although the analysis doesn't capture inherent variability of wind and solar.

  • "We feel that we're on very firm ground in an honest, competitive marketplace, but no industry can overcome active obstruction," Grumet said.

The big picture: The fight is unfolding as U.S. electricity demand rises rapidly, driven largely by the AI boom. That's a contradiction Grumet sees at the heart of Trump's energy policy.

  • "The imperative to repudiate renewables is a greater incentive than the imperative to lower energy costs," he said, calling that "outrageous."

The other side: "The issue the president has with wind and solar is, is it's not going to be the solution for the power needs that we have," Agen said, highlighting nuclear power instead.

  • He rejected the premise that the administration categorically opposes renewable energy, saying they shouldn't have received preferential subsidies and citing dependence on China for energy equipment.
  • A White House official said Tuesday night the administration and lawmakers had agreed to a "strong bipartisan" package, but warned that administration commitments "will not remain frozen indefinitely" if the deal doesn't advance quickly.

Zoom in: Pentagon delays in reviewing onshore wind projects are a key sticking point in the permitting debate.

  • "Just rubber-stamping every project to come in is not good," Agen said.
  • Grumet countered that legitimate military concerns can be addressed: "These are solvable problems."

After Congress accelerated the wind and solar tax credits' expiration last year, Grumet said the industry expected "some return to normalcy."

  • Instead, agencies took what ACP counts as at least 17 actions restricting development, including halting offshore wind leasing, adding political reviews to permits and delaying Pentagon reviews of onshore wind projects.

Catch up quick: Federal courts have blocked several of these moves, including the broad freeze on wind approvals, barriers to renewable permitting and Pentagon reviews.

What we're watching: Trump issued an executive order in August that could restrict certain electrical equipment with ties to China.

  • Depending on how broadly the Energy Department interprets it, Grumet said, "it has the potential to be devastating to the economy."

item.title: OpenAI debuts "dots" as industry safety focus shifts to "What did my AI assistant do now?"
item.description:
OpenAI is equipping high-end subscribers with always-on agents, known as dots. It's a bold move from a company that continues to deal with reports of its agents breaking past intended safeguards.

Why it matters: AI's safety challenge has moved from "Will the chatbot say something harmful?" to "How can we stop autonomous agents from attempting hacks online?" to "Uh-oh, what did my AI assistant do now?"

Driving the news: The unveiling of dots was the signature debut among a flurry of announcements at OpenAI's developer conference on Tuesday.

  • Think of a Dot as an AI assistant running on its own virtual computer in the cloud. It can browse the web, use connected apps, create files and run tools while keeping track of a project over time.
  • Dots can be summoned on mobile devices or computers and work across connected apps, browsers and their own virtual computer.

The big picture: Dots (like Meta's Muse) are being launched publicly despite a spate of revelations about agents from OpenAI and other AI companies taking unintended actions.

  • In just the last few days, OpenAI has been making fresh disclosures of unintended behavior and apologizing to Australia for hacking into its Medicare system's websites.
  • OpenAI also said this week it was scrapping an update to its most powerful Astra model after it failed to meet safety thresholds.

Between the lines: It's not the first time OpenAI has been at the center of safety concerns.

  • In the early days of ChatGPT, much of the focus was on the potential for dangerous discussions, such as encouraging suicide or eating disorders, issues for which OpenAI faces multiple lawsuits.
  • Now, the conversation is shifting to potentially harmful agentic actions. In the most serious security incident to date, OpenAI's agents were behind a July attack on Hugging Face.

What they're saying: OpenAI leaders expressed confidence that the dots it is sending into the world won't run amok. The company said dots include safeguards from ChatGPT and Codex, plus additional protections from a system internally called Guardian, known publicly as Auto-review.

  • By default, the new agents require people to approve significant actions. For example, a dot can draft a message but should not send it to another person or agent unless the user has asked it to do so, OpenAI member of product staff Alexander Embiricos told Axios. It also will not complete some consequential financial transactions, instead handing control back to the user.
  • "We're not going to do this for you, but we can take you all the way up until the point where you do it yourself, and we'll hand over to you," Embiricos said.
  • Another key part of OpenAI's strategy is limiting its initial rollout to a smaller group of its most faithful users before expanding. Dots are initially available to Pro, Business Premium and Enterprise users, with each person having a single assistant.

CEO Sam Altman said the goal is not to plow blindly forward nor to halt progress entirely, but instead to keep safety, alignment and monitoring ahead of advances in capability.

  • "My hope is that, in this industry, we can come together and say we need to get down this middle path," Altman told reporters.

item.title: U.S.-Iran talks yield little, raising odds of renewed combat
item.description:
Efforts this week by Qatari mediators to broker a diplomatic breakthrough between the U.S. and Iran have made little progress, with neither side willing to budge, according to three sources familiar with the talks.

Why it matters: The stalemate bolsters the belief on both sides that a renewed military conflict is becoming more likely. U.S. officials think President Trump could order a return to major combat operations after the midterms.

  • Qatari officials will keep trying, but they're growing increasingly frustrated with both sides, two of the sources said.

Driving the news: Qatari mediator Ali al-Thawadi met Monday with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and his team in New York for several hours.

  • A source with knowledge said they discussed a two-page Qatari compromise proposal.
  • According to two other sources, the Qatari plan was aimed at addressing both Iran's demand for lifting the U.S. naval blockade and the U.S. demand for Iranian nuclear concessions.
  • On Monday evening, al-Thawadi held talks in Washington with Trump envoy Jared Kushner and other U.S. officials. Vice President JD Vance also attended a small part of the meeting.
  • The White House declined to comment.

The intrigue: On Monday morning, the White House was hopeful of progress.

  • U.S. officials briefed several media outlets, including Axios, saying the talks were "positive and constructive" and that Iran "indicated they are flexible on the nuclear issues."
  • The officials even said Trump was willing to give Iran sanctions relief and release frozen funds in return for concrete steps to pare back its nuclear program.
  • But several hours later, while the Qatari officials were still at the White House, Trump posted on Truth Social that he offered nothing to Iran.

State of play: One of the sources said there was no significant movement in the talks on Monday.

  • "It is stuck. The Iranians are asking for things the U.S. can't accept and the U.S. thinks it is winning so there is no need for compromise," the source said.
  • Other regional mediators, including Pakistan and Egypt, urged Iran to agree to nuclear concessions. But the Iranians said they would only consider doing so after the U.S. agrees to return to the June memorandum of understanding, another source with knowledge said.

The other side: Iran's Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, said Tuesday that Iran has conveyed its terms to the U.S. but that "Trump is incapable of making a decision," per the Iranian press.

  • "Trump is trapped in a quagmire in which he can neither negotiate nor fight," Rezaei said.

"They are doing very poorly. I don't know if they are ready to give up yet. They will give up. This is to stop a nuclear weapon. Iran will not have a nuclear weapon," Trump told reporters on Tuesday.

item.title: Boeing nabs $20B contract for Navy's futuristic fighter
item.description:
Boeing will build the U.S. Navy's next fighter aircraft, following years of clandestine competition and multiple contracting false alarms.

Why it matters: Boeing's win in the F/A-XX competition means the company's sixth-generation aircraft will succeed the Super Hornet fleet, long relied upon and recently employed across the Middle East.

  • The company is also constructing the Air Force's F-47, previously unveiled in an Oval Office address featuring President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

The latest: The Pentagon announced the deal Tuesday. It's worth more than $20 billion.

  • It comes after months of squabbling between the White House, Pentagon, lawmakers and industry.
  • Its ups and downs and rumored award timelines were closely watched by defense analysts and reporters.

Context: Boeing bested Northrop Grumman. Lockheed Martin was previously knocked out of the running.

  • Executives from both companies had told Axios they were confident in their offerings.

State of play: Little has been revealed about the warplane's final design. But it will complement the F-35, of which there are short-takeoff and carrier variants.

What they're saying: Former Navy Secretary John Phelan in December told Axios that F/A-XX was, in fact, not dead. He previously told lawmakers the warplane would ensure naval air dominance.

  • Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle advocated for the project during his nomination hearing, telling lawmakers the service "must have an air wing that is comprised of the most advanced strike fighters."
  • And Caudle's predecessor, Lisa Franchetti, suggested it would sport "advanced sensors, advanced lethality, advanced range" and be able to "integrate with manned and unmanned capabilities."

More from Axios:

American airpower

F/A-XX decision must be "made quickly," Navy chief says

Trump administration shelves Navy's F/A-XX, citing industry strain

item.title: Trump floats Jay Clayton as AI czar as he looks to fill the position in days
item.description:
President Trump on Tuesday told Axios Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton would be a good AI czar.

Why it matters: Trump is actively looking to fill the position as calls for government intervention on AI intensify.

Driving the news: As the director of national intelligence, Clayton is the president's principle intelligence adviser that sits atop the 18-agency intelligence community.

  • During his July confirmation hearing, Clayton said that, similarly to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's approach, for the intelligence community "it resonates that AI is not only an opportunity but a threat."
  • "When something's both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it," Clayton said.

Asked who he wants to be AI czar, Trump said: "I have somebody in mind."

  • Clayton is "a good man. He's right here. That's a good idea," Trump added when prompted.

The precise duties of the czar have yet to be spelled out, although Trump earlier said he wants to create the AI Force, a new government agency.

  • Trump told reporters outside the White House he wants to pick someone in the next three or four days.
  • Trump, House Speaker Mike Johnson and AI executives met today to discuss balancing AI innovation and safety and encourage compoanies to regulate themselves and each other.

Catch up quick: Silicon Valley players and venture capitalist David Sacks, who also attended Tuesday's meeting, previously held the AI czar role.

  • Sacks left that post in March after his special government employee status ran out but continued to exert influence from an outside advisory role.
