item.title: "Washington is broken": Democrats running for office turn sharply against their own party
item.description:
Democrats are adopting a drastically more negative tone toward their own party in the 2026 midterm elections, swapping promises of bipartisan collaboration with vows to "take on corruption in both parties."

Why it matters: This surge in political friendly fire reflects the extraordinary level of anger candidates are seeing from their voters toward the Democratic Party and the national political establishment.

  • Sam Forstag, a House candidate in Montana, told Axios in an interview that "a whole lot of my coworkers got a sour look on their face" when he revealed he was running as a Democrat.
  • "We have heard pretty loud and clear, whether it's at our town halls or on parade routes, that ... there's just a growing frustration with both political parties," said Jake Johnson, a Democratic candidate in Minnesota.
Data: AdImpact; Note: Party totals include independents running as the de facto nominee; Chart: Andrew Solender/Axios

By the numbers: An Axios analysis of more than 350 ads in federal and statewide elections since 2018 found a huge uptick in Democratic ads mentioning either the Democratic Party or both parties in a negative context.

  • The analysis looked at ads run between Aug. 24 and Sept. 22 of each election year that used phrases such as "my own party," "both parties," and "party leaders."
  • Candidates often try to appeal to swing voters by pitching themselves as bipartisan problem solvers, pointing out past instances of collaboration or making pledges to work across the aisle if elected.
  • But Democrats have leaned hard into more populist, anti-establishment rhetoric this year, with ads denouncing a broken political system or citing past instances in which they defied their party.

"I didn't care that he was a Democrat or the pressure that I got to make it go away," Virginia Democrat Shannon Taylor says in one ad about the prosecution of former state Sen. Joe Morrissey.

  • Randy Villegas, a Democratic candidate in California, declares in one of his ads: "Washington is broken because corrupt politicians in both parties care more about their donors and their party bosses than us."
  • "I'll stand up to anyone, Democrat or Republican, who isn't focused on what's right for them," vows Blake Gendebien, a Democrat in upstate New York.

Even the House Democratic campaign arm is getting in on the action, running a coordinated ad with Michigan Democrat Christina Hines in which the former SVU prosecutor recounts how she "cleaned up messes when I put away predators, pedophiles, and murderers."

  • "I didn't care if they were Republican or Democrat," she says in the spot, adding that "right now, D.C. is the biggest mess of all."
  • Says Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio) in an ad: "Washington's not just broken, it's deeply corrupt, and both parties need to shape up."

Between the lines: Axios identified 47 ads run by Democrats or independents running as the de facto Democratic nominee in the last 30 days with that type of negative messaging, up from 19 in 2024 and 2022, 15 in 2020, and 14 in 2018.

  • Democrats' positive messaging about the two parties — such as promises to "work with both parties" or "bring Democrats and Republicans together" — has plummeted from 45 ads in 2024 to 18 this year.
  • That contrasts with Republicans' relatively cheery tone: "Republicans defending a broken status quo should be very nervous," said Eric Koch, a Democratic operative working on House races.

What they're saying: Forstag said he "can think of no better articulation of the literal disconnect between our representatives at the federal level and what it's been like on the ground" than Democrats' positive economic message in 2024.

  • "What I hear from people is that even the basic necessities are becoming more and more difficult to afford," the Montana Democrat told Axios.
  • Johnson pointed to Minnesota's sprawling fraud scandal as "a huge issue" that "really erodes peoples' trust" in the state's Democratic-led government.

"Everybody that I talk to, and this has become more and more true over the years, hates both parties," said Hines, "hates Democrats, hates Republicans."

  • Justin Pearson of Tennessee told Axios voters see "way too many similarities between the Democratic Party and Republican Party."
  • "Democrats have a responsibility to hold ourselves ... to a higher standard," Pearson added.

Yes, but: Some Democrats prefer to keep their cross-party messaging optimistic.

  • Swing-district Rep. Greg Landsman (D-Ohio) is running an ad lauding how he "got Republicans and Democrats to work together and change the law" on Social Security benefits for public pensioners.
  • "I really do believe that the opposite of this deeply unpopular status quo is people working together to get shit done," Landsman told Axios.

"I didn't care that he was a Democrat or the pressure that I got to make it go away," Virginia Democrat Shannon Taylor says in one ad about the prosecution of former state Sen. Joe Morrissey.

  • Randy Villegas, a Democratic candidate in California, declares in one of his ads: "Washington is broken because corrupt politicians in both parties care more about their donors and their party bosses than us."
  • "I'll stand up to anyone, Democrat or Republican, who isn't focused on what's right for them," vows Blake Gendebien, a Democrat in upstate New York.

Even the House Democratic campaign arm is getting in on the action, running a coordinated ad with Michigan Democrat Christina Hines in which the former SVU prosecutor recounts how she "cleaned up messes when I put away predators, pedophiles, and murderers."

  • "I didn't care if they were Republican or Democrat," she says in the spot, adding that "right now, D.C. is the biggest mess of all."
  • Says Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio) in an ad: "Washington's not just broken, it's deeply corrupt, and both parties need to shape up."

Between the lines: Axios identified 47 ads run by Democrats or independents running as the de facto Democratic nominee in the last 30 days with that type of negative messaging, up from 19 in 2024 and 2022, 15 in 2020, and 14 in 2018.

  • Democrats' positive messaging about the two parties — such as promises to "work with both parties" or "bring Democrats and Republicans together" — has plummeted from 45 ads in 2024 to 18 this year.
  • That contrasts with Republicans' relatively cheery tone: "Republicans defending a broken status quo should be very nervous," said Eric Koch, a Democratic operative working on House races.

What they're saying: Forstag said he "can think of no better articulation of the literal disconnect between our representatives at the federal level and what it's been like on the ground" than Democrats' positive economic message in 2024.

  • "What I hear from people is that even the basic necessities are becoming more and more difficult to afford," the Montana Democrat told Axios.
  • Johnson pointed to Minnesota's sprawling fraud scandal as "a huge issue" that "really erodes peoples' trust" in the state's Democratic-led government.

"Everybody that I talk to, and this has become more and more true over the years, hates both parties," said Hines, "hates Democrats, hates Republicans."

  • Justin Pearson of Tennessee told Axios voters see "way too many similarities between the Democratic Party and Republican Party."
  • "Democrats have a responsibility to hold ourselves ... to a higher standard," Pearson added.

Yes, but: Some Democrats prefer to keep their cross-party messaging optimistic.

  • Swing-district Rep. Greg Landsman (D-Ohio) is running an ad lauding how he "got Republicans and Democrats to work together and change the law" on Social Security benefits for public pensioners.
  • "I really do believe that the opposite of this deeply unpopular status quo is people working together to get shit done," Landsman told Axios.

item.title: Trump asked Xi to stop supporting Iran
item.description:
President Trump asked Chinese President Xi Jinping to halt any assistance to Iran when the two spoke during his state visit, U.S. Ambassador to Beijing David Perdue said Friday.

Why it matters: China's economic, intelligence and military support for Iran has undermined Trump's effort to isolate the country amid the ongoing war.

  • The U.S. is conducting a massive economic pressure campaign against Iran, but without Chinese cooperation it will only be partially effective.

Driving the news: U.S. officials have been concerned since the start of the war that China is supplying Iran with air defense systems and parts to build drones.

  • In recent weeks, Iran has used high-resolution imagery obtained from Chinese commercial satellites that allow it to target U.S. bases in the Middle East as well as aircraft carriers and other Navy ships in the Gulf and in Arabian Sea, U.S. officials say.
  • The discovery spurred the U.S. military to change its operational procedures to make it harder for Iran to locate and target Navy ships, a U.S. official said.

What they're saying: "We have made it very clear to them weeks ago that any help that they would give Iran, whether it be direct or indirect, whether it be intelligence or parts or military equipment was totally unacceptable. President Trump made that very clear again yesterday," Perdue said in an interview with CNBC on Friday.

  • Perdue said the U.S. told China that Iran is an independent issue that is not linked to Taiwan in any way.
  • "We have seen evidence that they have listened to us. They pulled some things down. We have evidence they pay attention when President Trump speaks about Iran," he said.

The other side: According to Chinese state media, Xi urged Trump to de-escalate with Iran by returning to the June memorandum of understanding and reaching a nuclear deal.

  • "China has encouraged relevant parties to stay committed to peaceful solutions and maintain the momentum of talks," Xi told Trump.

State of play: The meeting between Trump and Xi came a day after U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held a new round of indirect negotiations with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.

  • Qatari officials participated in the negotiations, passing messages between the two parties, sources with direct knowledge said.
  • The sources said Araghchi gave Witkoff and Kushner Iran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and resuming nuclear talks.
  • "It was the same terms the Iranians spoke about publicly before the meeting," the source said.
  • Iran proposed reopening the strait and resuming nuclear talks in a week, if the U.S. lifts its naval blockade, removes sanctions on oil sales and reinstates a ceasefire across the region.
  • The U.S. negotiators made it clear to the Iranians during the talks on Tuesday that Iran doesn't control the strait and therefore can't make demands about it.
  • Dozens of oil tankers are transiting the strait each day under U.S. protection, moving millions of barrels of oil to global markets — still well below pre-war volumes but enough to ease pressure.

What to watch: Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, who is the key mediator between Iran and the U.S., met Thursday in New York with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian to discuss the diplomatic effort.

  • A source with knowledge of the mediation efforts said Qatar and Iran are waiting to hear Trump's response to the Iranian proposal.
  • "It is still early to know where it is going, but there are some positive movements," the source said.

item.title: House Republicans on track to lose majority
item.description:
House Republicans are on track to lose their majority just a little over one month out from the midterm elections, according to a nonpartisan election forecaster.

Why it matters: Cook Political Report shifted 15 House races toward Democrats on Friday, the latest sign that the political environment is deteriorating for Republicans.

  • Democrats only need a net gain of three seats to take the majority.
  • Cook now projects Democrats are most likely to gain between five and 15 seats, which would give them a 220-230 seat majority next year.

The big picture: Republicans have spent much of the cycle arguing that redistricting and a sizable financial advantage would give them more breathing room.

  • But new Democratic maps in California and Utah are largely offsetting Republicans' redistricting gains elsewhere, according to Cook.
  • Republicans still hold a financial edge over Democrats. The National Republican Congressional Committee entered the final stretch with $13 million more in cash on hand than the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee — a record advantage for this point in the cycle.

State of play: Democrats are favored in 208 races, compared with 205 for Republicans after Friday's ratings changes.

  • There are now 17 Republican-held seats rated as Toss Ups, compared with just five Democratic-held seats.
  • Republicans would need to win a majority of the Toss Up races to keep control of the House, according to Cook.

Zoom out: Some of the most competitive House races are overwhelmingly in districts President Trump won in 2024.

  • Trump is underwater in many of those districts, driven in large part by dissatisfaction with his handling of the economy, according to Cook.
  • The median Toss Up district voted for Trump by 7 percentage points in 2024.

What they're saying: "Nobody outside the D.C. bubble cares what a bunch of pundits slap on a race rating," NRCC spokesman Mike Marinella told Axios in a statement.

  • "House races are won in the districts, and Republicans have the stronger ground game, air superiority across the battleground, and historic financial firepower while Democrats are still begging for cash just to prop up their socialist bailout fund."
  • DCCC Communications Director Courtney Rice told Axios: "The floor is falling out from underneath House Republicans. After two years of raising costs and lying to the American people, they've all but assured that they will lose the majority in November."

Editor's note: This story has been updated with comment from the NRCC and DCCC.

item.title: ICE wasted millions in rush to expand detention, government watchdog finds
item.description:
ICE has received more than $75 billion to expand operations since President Trump returned to office — and wasted millions on scaled-back and mismanaged projects, a new GAO report found.

Why it matters: In rushing to execute Trump's mass deportation agenda, the agency failed to properly develop a strategic plan, according to the Government Accountability Office report.

Driving the news: The report found that ICE invested billions in six new initiatives without conducting necessary analyses.

  • The report concluded that "[i]n the absence of a comprehensive strategic plan to guide detention expansion, ICE has wasted funds on unsuccessful detention initiatives and lacks important information about the long-term affordability of its investments."
  • For example, the agency purchased more than $2.5 billion in detention facilities and warehouses but didn't calculate how much the properties would cost to maintain after the first three years, when its current federal funding will expire without additional congressional authorization.

Catch up quick: ICE received an unprecedented amount of money to bolster operations, including $45 billion through the One Big Beautiful Bill in 2025 and more than $31 billion from the Secure America Act in June 2026.

  • That additional funding helped increase ICE's daily detained population by 71% between January 2025 and July 2026.

By the numbers: ICE rushed to purchase 11 warehouses to be converted into immigration facilities, but in June 2026, ICE officials told GAO that they were going to sell seven of them.

  • The reported cost of all 11 warehouses was roughly $1.07 billion. The sell-off caused ICE to lose about $7.7 million in nonrecoverable purchasing costs, such as zoning assessments.
  • ICE continues to pay utilities and security costs at these locations, costing an additional $12.8 million, per August estimates.
  • The agency also spent $7.1 million on unneeded meals at Fort Bliss because the vendor contract didn't allow for fluctuations in occupancy levels. At Guantanamo Bay, the Defense Department spent $2.85 million assembling tents that were never used after Homeland Security determined they "did not meet detention standards."

What they're saying: "The costs cited in the GAO report were appropriate and necessary to execute valid real property acquisition transactions and to ensure the properties are properly protected and maintained post-acquisition," a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson emailed Axios.

  • "From day one, DHS has remained singularly focused on removing the worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens from the United States and is always evaluating the best methods to do so."
  • "These heinous criminals, once arrested, should be removed at lightning speed, not housed on American soil at the taxpayer's expense. DHS is moving swiftly to utilize EXISTING detention space with our state and county partners."

Zoom out: In some cases, the agency bypassed its normal contracting procedures, without negotiating costs.

  • At the since-shuttered, so-called Alligator Alcatraz in Florida, the bed rate was $249 per day, approximately 171% higher than ICE's median rate of $92.

What we're watching: GAO recommended ICE develop a comprehensive strategic plan, and DHS agreed.

  • But ICE projected that the plan won't be completed until Aug. 31, 2027, prompting GAO to conclude that given the "potential for continued waste of taxpayer dollars, more timely completion may be warranted."
  • The White House referred Axios to DHS for a request to comment. DHS did not respond to repeated requests for comment.

Go deeper: ICE targets Plan B after backlash to mega-jails plan

Editor's note: This story was updated with a comment from DHS.

item.title: Bill Gates warns AI is powerful enough to cause "a billion deaths"
item.description:
Bill Gates will warn on this weekend's "Meet the Press" that he can see a future where AI wipes out humanity.

Why it matters: Gates, one of technology's leading optimists, has increasingly sounded the alarm on AI dangers. His new comments come as techology leaders and the government weight how to handle fears of an AI-created doomsday.

Driving the news: "AI is certainly powerful enough to drive events that, you know, cause a billion deaths," he will tell Kristen Welker on "Meet the Press" on Sunday, per excerpts NBC released Friday.

  • "Even though it's pretty hard to get to 100%, there's never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people with ill intent using the latest AI tools."

Zoom out: Gates released a memo in August that defined AI as a technology more consequential than virtually any other in history.

  • In the essay, he argued that "AI will either be the greatest equalizer ever invented, or the worst source of injustice."
  • "On the current course and speed, there's a very high chance of a net negative outcome," he said.

What's next: Gates says that government and political parties need to work together now to find ways to keep AI from spiraling out of control.

item.title: 3 big questions as GOP nears moment of truth
item.description:
With midterms 39 days away and the outlook for President Trump's party looking increasingly bleak, top Republicans say they're focused on three big questions for the final stretch:

  1. Are their attack ads working? Republicans expect a wave of private polling in early October to reveal whether their massive financial advantage is cutting into Democrats' leads.
  • GOP groups had spent more than $450 million through Sept. 23, more than twice what Democrats had spent, according to campaign finance expert Rob Pyers.

But Republican strategists say they aren't sure yet whether the barrage is working amid voter anger over high prices, data centers and Trump's war in Iran.

  • Trump's political operation didn't begin pouring its $416 million war chest into attack ads until around Labor Day, and Republicans argue the ads need time to sink in.
  • Strategists are particularly watching the Texas Senate race, where national GOP groups have sunk more than $100 million into helping Ken Paxton against Democrat James Talarico. Several polls have shown Paxton — whom GOP leaders have long viewed as a problematic nominee — trailing Talarico.

"September tests whether your messaging moves the needle in races — and early October is when the map locks in," a Republican strategist told Axios.

2. Who gets cut loose? Republicans concede they'll have to make painful spending decisions by early October.

  • That could complicate things for GOP Senate contenders Mike Collins in Georgia and Michael Whatley in North Carolina, who have consistently trailed Democrats Jon Ossoff and Roy Cooper despite millions in Republicans' spending.

If Collins and Whatley's numbers don't improve, Republicans say they could redirect money to Michigan and New Hampshire, where the party is playing offense.

  • Republicans also may have to spend more in traditionally red states such as Kansas, where polls show GOP Sen. Roger Marshall in a tight race against Democrat Adam Hamilton.
  • Hamilton would be the first Kansas Democrat to win a Senate seat since 1932. The race is tight enough to have drawn Vice President Vance to the state for a recent visit to try to give Marshall a boost.

Trump's political operation, meanwhile, has begun spending to defend a South Carolina House district that Trump carried by 13 points in 2024.

3. What does Trump do? The president and his political team remain one of the midterms' biggest question marks.

  • Trump's team said early this year that he'd campaign weekly for GOP candidates. That didn't happen. Trump now says he'll spend the final 30 days campaigning for candidates in 35 key Senate and House races.
  • By early October, Republican strategists expect to see whether he'll follow through — and, if he does, where he goes.

Where Trump doesn't go could be just as telling. Some Republicans in competitive races are keeping their distance from the unpopular administration.

  • When Vance visited Iowa last week, GOP Senate candidate Ashley Hinson didn't appear, citing previously scheduled events.
  • Then there's the question of how much Trump's willing to spend. Strategists say that should become clear in early October.

item.title: Debate-shy: Candidates aren't sharing the stage like they used to
item.description:
Debates in political campaigns used to be a given. Today, candidates increasingly view them as optional — or a political liability to be avoided.

Why it matters: In a midterm cycle dominated by unprecedented spending on contrast ads, the candidates themselves are remarkably reluctant to challenge each other face-to-face.

  • It's a sign of how campaigns have evolved, and an erosion of norms: Candidates — fueled by their parties and super PACs — still try to tear apart the opposition, they just do it from a distance.
  • In the age of short, shareable video clips, TV debates offer candidates equal parts opportunity and risk: An electric moment can travel far and wide, but so can an unforced error.

By the numbers: In 10 of the most closely watched races for governor, there are no agreed-upon debates between the major-party nominees in half of them — Arizona, Florida, Nevada, Ohio and Texas, according to an Axios review of scheduled debates.

  • Four years ago, just two of those 10 gubernatorial contests went without a debate.
  • In 10 tight Senate races this year, there are no debates scheduled in three states — North Carolina, Ohio and Texas. That's up from one debate-free race in the same seats last time around.
  • Some campaigns are still dickering over possible venues and moderators, and more debates could be added closer to the Nov. 3 election.

Driving the news: Florida's Democratic nominee for governor, David Jolly, became the latest official no-show when he said Sunday that he wouldn't debate Republican Rep. Byron Donalds.

  • "I think he's acting with bad faith and continues to peddle lies," Jolly said. "You can't debate a liar."
  • Donalds called Jolly "scared."
  • This is would be the first time since 1974 that Florida hasn't had a debate among contenders for governor. Neither Jolly not Donalds debated their primary opponents.

Zoom out: Jolly's debate dodge — unexpected for a financially outgunned Democrat running in a red state— is part of a broader pattern in which challengers and incumbents are making strategic decisions not to debate.

  • In some cases, they enumerate their reasons. In others, they aren't offering much of an explanation.

In Ohio, Democratic gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton is refusing to debate Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, citing personal attacks against her and her family.

  • "I will not be giving a platform to someone who I think is not just out of touch and not right, for I think he is a danger," Acton said.

In Texas, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who debated Democratic challenger Beto O'Rourke in 2022, hasn't agreed to debate Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa this year. No explanation given.

In Nevada, Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford says he's accepted two invitations to debate Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo. But Lombardo hasn't publicly committed to them — or commented about it.

Yes, but: One state stands out from the rest, Iowa. It had one gubernatorial debate in 2022, but has four scheduled this fall, a sign of how hotly contested the Republican-led state has become as support for Trump and his policies has cratered in farm country.

The intrigue: Arizona Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs is one of the few candidates who's declined to debate this year and also declined to debate her opponent four years ago. But she's tweaked her rationale.

  • In 2022, when she faced Republican Kari Lake, Hobbs argued that Lake, a Trump loyalist, would turn a debate into a spectacle, with "constant interruptions, pointless distractions, and childish name-calling."
  • This year, Hobbs is refusing to debate Republican Rep. Andy Biggs, offering a new explanation: Her campaign says engaging directly with Arizonans is more effective than a debate stage built for "short soundbites and political theater."

Zoom in: Even the Senate — an institution built around debate — isn't immune.

  • In Texas, Democratic state Rep. James Talarico has accepted invitations to three televised debates against Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton. Paxton's campaign says he'll debate Talarico but hasn't committed to any of the proposed events. (On Thursday, Talarico challenged Paxton to debate on Fox News, which he called "Ken Paxton's safe space.")
  • In North Carolina, neither former Gov. Roy Cooper (D) nor Michael Whatley, a former Republican National Committee chair, have accepted any of at least three debate invitations, although both have indicated they're open to debating.
  • In Ohio, former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) said he assumes he'll debate Republican Sen. Jon Husted, but nothing has been scheduled.

What they're saying: Brett O'Donnell, a veteran GOP debate-prep consultant, said the disappearance of debates is bad for democracy, but it's a sign of how the campaign and media landscape are changing.

  • "There's so much more money in campaigns now, and a way to get messages out on social media," he said.
  • "We live in a world where people get impatient after watching something for 15 seconds online," O'Donnell added. "How many people will actually watch an hour-long debate?"
item.content:encoded:
Debates in political campaigns used to be a given. Today, candidates increasingly view them as optional — or a political liability to be avoided.

Why it matters: In a midterm cycle dominated by unprecedented spending on contrast ads, the candidates themselves are remarkably reluctant to challenge each other face-to-face.

  • It's a sign of how campaigns have evolved, and an erosion of norms: Candidates — fueled by their parties and super PACs — still try to tear apart the opposition, they just do it from a distance.
  • In the age of short, shareable video clips, TV debates offer candidates equal parts opportunity and risk: An electric moment can travel far and wide, but so can an unforced error.

By the numbers: In 10 of the most closely watched races for governor, there are no agreed-upon debates between the major-party nominees in half of them — Arizona, Florida, Nevada, Ohio and Texas, according to an Axios review of scheduled debates.

  • Four years ago, just two of those 10 gubernatorial contests went without a debate.
  • In 10 tight Senate races this year, there are no debates scheduled in three states — North Carolina, Ohio and Texas. That's up from one debate-free race in the same seats last time around.
  • Some campaigns are still dickering over possible venues and moderators, and more debates could be added closer to the Nov. 3 election.

Driving the news: Florida's Democratic nominee for governor, David Jolly, became the latest official no-show when he said Sunday that he wouldn't debate Republican Rep. Byron Donalds.

  • "I think he's acting with bad faith and continues to peddle lies," Jolly said. "You can't debate a liar."
  • Donalds called Jolly "scared."
  • This is would be the first time since 1974 that Florida hasn't had a debate among contenders for governor. Neither Jolly not Donalds debated their primary opponents.

Zoom out: Jolly's debate dodge — unexpected for a financially outgunned Democrat running in a red state— is part of a broader pattern in which challengers and incumbents are making strategic decisions not to debate.

  • In some cases, they enumerate their reasons. In others, they aren't offering much of an explanation.

In Ohio, Democratic gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton is refusing to debate Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, citing personal attacks against her and her family.

  • "I will not be giving a platform to someone who I think is not just out of touch and not right, for I think he is a danger," Acton said.

In Texas, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who debated Democratic challenger Beto O'Rourke in 2022, hasn't agreed to debate Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa this year. No explanation given.

item.title: Meta's new motto: we care about privacy
item.description:
Meta is seeking to make privacy protections a centerpiece of new products including its viral assistant Muse, marking a major shift for a company built on extensive use of customer data.

Why it matters: The radical turnaround is an acknowledgment that the winner of AI's new assistant race will have to reassure users that they can turn over their emails, finances, health data and other sensitive information.

  • Without that, a super-intelligent personal agent is essentially useless.

Driving the news: Meta, whose privacy policy once allowed it nearly unfettered access to use almost everything people did with Meta AI (in almost any way it wanted), has made a significant shift in recent months to put privacy at the center of its AI strategy.

  • In a 6,500-word August manifesto, CEO Mark Zuckerberg laid out a broad promise. "We believe that people should have a fully private mode for personal agents where even Meta or any other service provider cannot see or grant access to your information."
  • With Muse, which appears to be on a path to becoming one of the most popular AI hits since ChatGPT, the company is offering all customers their own personal virtual machine. A soon-to-be-available option would ensure that even Meta won't have access to the data.
  • Meta is also readying a similar "private processing" option for interactions with its AI glasses.

Small efforts have been underway for more than a year, starting with the addition of incognito chats and private processing, which arrived first in WhatsApp, where Meta also provides end-to-end encryption. More recently, the options have spread to other Meta apps.

Yes, but: Customers still have to pay close attention if they want to minimize the amount of data shared with Meta. In Muse, for example, the default setting allows interactions to be used for training the company's AI models, though that can be turned off.

  • And not all of the privacy changes being offered to Muse users apply to those accessing Meta AI in other ways, such as through the Facebook, Instagram or Meta AI apps.
  • Plus, Meta devices continue to spur other types of privacy concerns.
  • "Meta's products that embed microphones and cameras in everyday devices pose serious privacy risks to people just trying to live their lives and go about their day without being recorded or surveilled," Electronic Privacy Information Center executive director Alan Butler told Axios. "Confidential processing doesn't solve the problem of pushing embedded surveillance systems out into the world."

The big picture: Meta has spent years building a thriving business based on tapping extensive knowledge about its customers to serve up content and ads that it knows will be right up their alley.

  • Its practices have also drawn lawsuits from a wide range of entities that say Meta designed social media to be addictive and caused harm.

How it works: Meta is betting on a new business model to fund Muse, which won't provide the same data for targeted advertising that supports most of the company's services. Muse has $20- and $100-per-month paid tiers for heavy users, but Meta expects the free tier to account for most usage.

  • "We believe that Muse will make you money, and we're standing behind this by making Muse free for a huge number of tokens, with the expectation that over time we will profit by taking a small fee from transactions," Zuckerberg said.

Our thought bubble: There's still a trust gap based on Meta's years of gobbling up nearly all the data it could. That can't be addressed with words, but requires establishing a new track record.

item.title: Senate Democrats put Trump's D.C. makeover on notice
item.description:
Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) plans to force a Senate vote next week on two new resolutions aimed at preventing President Trump from demolishing the Kennedy Center or building his proposed triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery.

Why it matters: Senate Democrats are putting Republicans on notice that they're prepared to use every available legislative means, including the appropriations process later this year, to stymie Trump's efforts to erect or erase memorials in the D.C. area.

Driving the news: Merkley will introduce his two bills when the Senate returns next week and then seek unanimous consent to consider them at the first opportunity.

  • That's likely to fail, but Democrats will have the procedural upper hand at the end of the year in the appropriations process, making individual votes more likely.
  • Merkley has an important ally in Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), who is cosponsoring Merkley's measure designed to protect the Kennedy Center. Both are on the Appropriations Subcommittee on Interior, Environment and Related Agencies.

Flashback: This spring, Republicans blinked when they faced pressure from Democrats over funding for Trump's new East Wing ballroom.

  • At the White House's request, Senate Republicans initially proposed $1 billion for the Secret Service for "above-ground and below-ground security features," but ultimately removed the language when it became clear they didn't have the votes.

The other side: Trump has said his arch will become a dual-use facility housing snipers, drones and ammunition.

  • When he closed the Kennedy Center for renovations, he called it "tired, broken and dilapidated" and in need of an upgrade.

Zoom in: Merkley's Kennedy Center measure is written broadly to prohibit the demolition of any presidential memorial designated by Congress, extending its protections to the Lincoln and Jefferson memorials.

  • "A memorial to honor a President of the United States designated by an Act of Congress may not be demolished unless authorized by an Act of Congress," the measure reads.
  • It defines "demolish" as "the intentional razing, destroying, or wrecking of an entire building or structure or a substantial portion of a building or structure."
  • Merkley's measure targeting Trump's planned arch is more specific. It would prohibit the use of federal funds "for the planning and construction of any structure or monument at Memorial Circle at Columbia Island/Lady Bird Johnson Park."

Zoom out: Democrats and conservative groups have so far largely relied on the courts to thwart Trump's plans for the Kennedy Center.

  • Last week, a federal judge ordered Trump officials to provide 30 days' written notice before making changes to the Kennedy Center, "including but not limited to any demolition" of the main building.
  • Trump's plans for the 250-foot arch are also being litigated. A veterans-led coalition is seeking to block construction, arguing that the project requires congressional authorization.

item.title: Scoop: NRSC pleads for $9M to defend three red seats
item.description:
The Senate GOP campaign arm is making an extraordinary late ask — $8.9 million, to be exact — for three red states: Alaska, Iowa and Ohio, according to a memo sent Thursday and obtained by Axios.

Why it matters: The request is yet another sign of the headwinds facing Republicans. In a good year, they wouldn't be begging for millions to defend states President Trump carried by double digits in 2024.

  • "We need $8.9 million in additional hard dollars to close the media gap and sustain that progress through Election Day," a memo from the National Republican Senatorial Committee states.

Zoom in: The memo lays out specific fundraising goals for each race, sending donors to joint fundraising accounts and campaigns.

  • $1.2 million in Alaska, where Democratic nominee former Rep. Mary Peltola leads Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) in the RealClearPolitics polling average by two percentage points.
  • $4.2 million in Iowa, where Democratic nominee Josh Turek and GOP nominee Rep. Ashley Hinson are separated by less than a percentage point in the RCP polling average.
  • $3.5 million in Ohio, where former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) has built a four-percentage-point lead over Sen. Jon Husted (R) in the RCP polling average.

Between the lines: The memo directs donors to candidates' campaigns or joint fundraising committees, which have higher donor limits.

  • The committee has been taking advantage of a Supreme Court ruling to get more advertising at lower prices by coordinating with campaigns.
  • NRSC Chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) touted this strategy in a closed-door lunch on Wednesday, showing in a chart how it has allowed them to keep up with Democrats' stronger campaign fundraising, according to slides seen by Axios.
  • "The environment remains tough, but these races have improved as the Republican ecosystem has engaged," says the NRSC memo.

Zoom out: Cook Political Report this week moved the Senate races in Georgia, Kansas and South Carolina in their ratings toward Democrats.

  • Sabato's Crystal Ball moved Kansas, Michigan and Iowa toward Democrats.
  • Democrats are competitive (at least lean-Republican) in seven seats currently held by Republicans, according to both raters.
  • They only need four to take the majority next Congress.

The other side: Democrats have their own late-stage headaches, with Democratic senators calling for a cash infusion for their candidate in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed — warning that he's getting trounced by outside super PACs.

What we're hearing: Republicans are quietly starting to count out North Carolina and Georgia, based on our conversations.

  • Semafor reported millions of dollars in GOP super PAC money were pulled from North Carolina.
  • But the GOP sees a silver lining in New Hampshire and Michigan, where their candidates are making competitive bids to flip Democratic seats.
  • Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is telling candidates to run the race they need to in their state, even if it means breaking with him, Congress, or, in some cases, President Trump.

The bottom line: "I'm very realistic about there are political headwinds for us, and so you have to navigate that," Thune told Axios on Wednesday.

item.title: White House reinstates access for banned reporters
item.description:
Reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were readmitted to the White House for the first time since Friday, hours after a judge ordered the Trump administration to immediately reinstate their credentials.

Why it matters: The reinstatement should mark the end of a broader press boycott that left the American public without key visual coverage of President Trump over the past few days.

State of play: As of 1pm ET, it was unclear whether television pool cameras would be in place to cover President Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

  • The major networks in the rotating television pool were still waiting on confirmation from the White House that CNN would be allowed to manage those duties.

Catch up quick: CNN, MS NOW, and Politico on Monday filed a First Amendment lawsuit against the White House, arguing the president and the administration violated their rights by blocking their access over the weekend.

  • Outlets that weren't banned but stood in solidarity with their peers vowed to suspend video and photo distribution until their peers' access was reinstated.
  • The judge overseeing the hearing, Trump appointee Timothy J. Kelly, ruled early Thursday morning that the administration had likely violated the outlets' Fifth Amendment rights and granted a temporary restraining order mandating their access be restored for 14 days.
  • In his ruling, Kelly said the plaintiffs "have shown a likelihood of success, at least on their Fifth Amendment procedural due process claim."

Zoom in: Later Thursday, reporters from the outlets were denied access despite the court order.

  • CNN, MS NOW and Politico subsequently requested an immediate hearing, noting the urgency given Xi's scheduled visit to the White House.
  • In a filing midday Thursday, director of White House press operations Micah Stopperich explained the administration were notified of the order to restore credentials at 7:10am ET and began that process at 7:25 am ET.
  • He said the confiscated badges were available for reporters to pick up starting at 9:55am ET.

What's next: Kelly declined to hold a hearing Thursday and set a Sept. 28 deadline for plaintiffs to file for a preliminary injunction which would maintain the news outlets' access while the case is litigated.

  • The brief order noted Kelly "intends to rule expeditiously on the motion for a preliminary injunction."
  • The White House previously indicated it would appeal the ruling, but it can't legally do so for the next two weeks.
  • If the case moves forward, the White House could seek an appeal. Kelly's decision doesn't address the plaintiff's First Amendment claims. Those are likely to be further litigated.

Disclosure: The author of this article is a paid contributor for CNN.

Editor's note: This story was updated throughout to reflect CNN, MS NOW and Politico have been reinstated.

item.title: AI's never-before-seen capital grab
item.description:
A new analysis of the AI buildout shows its staggering scale: $10.3 trillion in estimated AI infrastructure investment through 2032.

  • That amounts to 3.6% of GDP a year, dwarfing the investment booms that built America's railroads, highways, electric grid and telecom networks.

Why it matters: The AI boom has become far too big and too costly for even the largest tech companies to finance alone. This has resulted in trillions of dollars in demand for outside capital — and the potential risks that come along with that, according to new research being presented Friday at the Brookings Papers on Economic Activity.

  • Financing the buildout will require tapping bond markets, banks and private credit on a massive scale, adding to the flood of debt competing for investors' money at a time when borrowing costs are already surging.
  • So far, those higher costs appear to be doing little to curb the industry's appetite to build. The knock-on effect: The more capital the buildout absorbs, the greater the potential pressure on borrowing costs elsewhere in the economy.
  • In effect, any other entity that needs capital — from the U.S. government financing its $2 trillion per year deficit to an individual seeking a home mortgage or car loan — is in competition for funds with these hyperscalers.

What they're saying: Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, a Columbia Business School professor behind the new paper on how the AI infrastructure boom is being financed, says the industry's appetite for investment remains remarkably resilient to higher rates.

  • "They are so gung-ho to build these things" that even recent rate hikes and historically high long-term yields won't "deter too much of that development," Van Nieuwerburgh told reporters recently.
  • Morgan Stanley estimates that Big Tech will need roughly $2.9 trillion to expand its computing capacity through 2028 — with more than half coming from outside investors, according to the paper.

Case in point: Facebook parent Meta chose to finance most of its $30 billion Hyperion data center through outside investors, even though doing so meant paying substantially more to borrow.

  • The project's debt carries an interest rate at least 1 percentage point higher than Meta likely would have paid on its own debt, adding more than $5 billion in costs over the life of the deal, the paper estimates.

Threat level: The surge of outside money — much of it from private credit — allows the AI boom to keep scaling. But it spreads possible risks across the financial system, often through financing structures that are harder for investors and regulators to track.

  • The infrastructure would need to generate $3.7 trillion in annual revenue in the next six years to earn a 10% return — roughly 9% of GDP.
  • "The risks have been spreading throughout the financial system," Van Nieuwerburgh said, as the industry taps pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, private credit and other sources of outside capital.
  • "With that expansion comes more complexity, more opacity, and it's becoming difficult to track where the risks are being distributed," he said. "These risks are coming to a pension fund near you, so to speak."

What to watch: Van Nieuwerburgh says the influx of outside capital risks allowing the buildout to race ahead of actual demand.

  • "Sooner or later, we're going to have oversupply, just like we do in every real estate cycle, and then the prices will collapse," he said. "I don't see why this time is different."

The bottom line: The AI investment boom is now a major force in the broader economy, boosting growth while putting new pressure on capital markets and the financial system.

  • "This AI buildout is by far the largest ... it's 50% larger than the second-largest, which was the railroad buildout," Van Nieuwerburgh said.
item.content:encoded:
A new analysis of the AI buildout shows its staggering scale: $10.3 trillion in estimated AI infrastructure investment through 2032.

  • That amounts to 3.6% of GDP a year, dwarfing the investment booms that built America's railroads, highways, electric grid and telecom networks.

Why it matters: The AI boom has become far too big and too costly for even the largest tech companies to finance alone. This has resulted in trillions of dollars in demand for outside capital — and the potential risks that come along with that, according to new research being presented Friday at the Brookings Papers on Economic Activity.

  • Financing the buildout will require tapping bond markets, banks and private credit on a massive scale, adding to the flood of debt competing for investors' money at a time when borrowing costs are already surging.
  • So far, those higher costs appear to be doing little to curb the industry's appetite to build. The knock-on effect: The more capital the buildout absorbs, the greater the potential pressure on borrowing costs elsewhere in the economy.
  • In effect, any other entity that needs capital — from the U.S. government financing its $2 trillion per year deficit to an individual seeking a home mortgage or car loan — is in competition for funds with these hyperscalers.

What they're saying: Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, a Columbia Business School professor behind the new paper on how the AI infrastructure boom is being financed, says the industry's appetite for investment remains remarkably resilient to higher rates.

  • "They are so gung-ho to build these things" that even recent rate hikes and historically high long-term yields won't "deter too much of that development," Van Nieuwerburgh told reporters recently.
  • Morgan Stanley estimates that Big Tech will need roughly $2.9 trillion to expand its computing capacity through 2028 — with more than half coming from outside investors, according to the paper.

Case in point: Facebook parent Meta chose to finance most of its $30 billion Hyperion data center through outside investors, even though doing so meant paying substantially more to borrow.

  • The project's debt carries an interest rate at least 1 percentage point higher than Meta likely would have paid on its own debt, adding more than $5 billion in costs over the life of the deal, the paper estimates.

Threat level: The surge of outside money — much of it from private credit — allows the AI boom to keep scaling. But it spreads possible risks across the financial system, often through financing structures that are harder for investors and regulators to track.

  • The infrastructure would need to generate $3.7 trillion in annual revenue in the next six years to earn a 10% return — roughly 9% of GDP.
  • "The risks have been spreading throughout the financial system," Van Nieuwerburgh said, as the industry taps pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, private credit and other sources of outside capital.
  • "With that expansion comes more complexity, more opacity, and it's becoming difficult to track where the risks are being distributed," he said. "These risks are coming to a pension fund near you, so to speak."

What to watch: Van Nieuwerburgh says the influx of outside capital risks allowing the buildout to race ahead of actual demand.

  • "Sooner or later, we're going to have oversupply, just like we do in every real estate cycle, and then the prices will collapse," he said. "I don't see why this time is different."

The bottom line: The AI investment boom is now a major force in the broader economy, boosting growth while putting new pressure on capital markets and the financial system.

  • "This AI buildout is by far the largest ... it's 50% larger than the second-largest, which was the railroad buildout," Van Nieuwerburgh said.

item.title: Trump and Xi's summit revives panda diplomacy
item.description:
Chinese President Xi Jinping said Thursday during a visit with President Trump that China will send two pandas to Zoo Atlanta, calling them an "envoy of friendship."

Why it matters: The fuzzy ambassadors have long been one of China's most beloved tools of soft power and could signal an attempt to cool tensions in U.S.–China relations.

Driving the news: Xi made the remarks Thursday during his three-day visit to D.C., where he and Trump are expected to discuss AI, economic ties and critical minerals before a state dinner.

  • Trump hailed their "truly great friendship" and greeted Xi on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews earlier Thursday, a rare move not usually offered to heads of state visiting the U.S.

Zoom in: China typically loans pandas abroad for set terms as a sign of goodwill, and these pandas would be the first at Zoo Atlanta since its previous pandas returned to China in 2024.

  • Zoo Atlanta confirmed to Axios on Thursday that the pandas Xi mentioned are the same ones the zoo and the China Wildlife Conservation Association announced in April.
  • Male Ping Ping and female Fu Shuang are both from China's Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding.

Zoom out: China has also used its pandas as a cudgel when foreign relationships turn frosty.

  • Pandas living at the National Zoo in D.C. returned to China in 2023 when their agreement expired, as Washington and Beijing butted heads over security, economic and humanitarian issues. Two new pandas returned a year later under a new agreement.
  • Wild giant pandas are native to China, meaning other nations wishing to observe them typically must receive them from Beijing.

Flashback: The National Zoo's first pandas arrived during President Nixon and First Lady Pat Nixon made a historic trip to China in 1972 that opened a new chapter in U.S.–China relations.

  • At a dinner in Beijing, Pat told Chinese officials she had fallen in love with the furballs, and Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai replied, "I'll give you some."
  • Two months later, they arrived, and Pat predicted there would be "panda-monium" at the zoo — and she was right. Ling-Ling and Hsing-Hsing were the zoo's top attractions until they died in the 1990s.

Watch:

Go deeper: "Envoys of friendship": China set to send giant pandas to San Diego Zoo

item.title: White House ordered to restore access to banned news outlets
item.description:
A district court judge ruled the White House violated the Fifth Amendment rights of CNN, MS NOW and Politico by banning them, and granted the plaintiffs a temporary restraining order that forces the White House to immediately reinstate their press access for 14 days.

  • But both CNN and Politico said their reporters were denied access to the White House Thursday morning after the ruling.

Why it matters: Had a judge ruled against them, the broader press boycott could've dragged on, leaving the American public without key visual coverage of the White House.

  • Outlets that weren't banned but stood in solidarity with their peers vowed to suspend video and photo distribution until their peers' access was reinstated.

Zoom in: In a court filing Wednesday, district judge Timothy J. Kelly, a Trump appointee, said the plaintiffs "have shown a likelihood of success, at least on their Fifth Amendment procedural due process claim."

  • "The 'general rule,' is that 'individuals must receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before the Government deprives them' of a constitutionally protected interest," he noted.

Yes, but: CNN said a reporter and photojournalist were denied access early Thursday, though one producer was allowed in.

  • Politico said the Secret Service seized the press pass of a reporter who was denied access as well.

Context: The ruling comes ahead of a meeting at the White House between President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, which means journalists will be able to cover the event and the public will get access to video and photography coverage.

Zoom out: The decision marks a huge win for the media, as it reinforces previous precedents set around its Fifth Amendment rights.

  • In their complaint, the outlets argued the White House violated their First Amendment rights by blocking them in retaliation for their reporting and discriminating against their viewpoint; and their Fifth Amendment rights for banning them without due process.

What they're saying: "This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law. We greatly appreciate the court's swift action." Theodore J. Boutrous, Jr., attorney for CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, said in a statement.

Flashback: Kelly oversaw a CNN lawsuit against the White House for blocked access in 2018.

  • In that case, he granted CNN a temporary restraining order that required the White House restore then-correspondent Jim Acosta's press badge, ruling that the White House violated his Fifth Amendment rights by pulling his credentials without notice or an appeal process.
  • While outcome of that case isn't binding, it does hold weight in informing Kelly's decision-making. CNN, MS NOW and Politico referenced that case in their lawsuit.

Zoom out: Press freedom lawyers argue the plaintiffs have a strong First Amendment case, given a binding legal precedent set by a higher court.

  • In 1977, a federal appeals court ruled that the White House could not revoke a journalist's press credentials based on their coverage or viewpoint.
  • In that case, journalist Robert Sherrill sued the White House for being denied a press pass with no explanation.
  • That court ruled that once the White House opens up space as a public forum and lets journalists in, it cannot selectively remove access for select reporters based on their viewpoint or coverage under the First Amendment.

What's next: The judge will hear more evidence from the plaintiffs and defendants for the next two weeks, after which time, an appeal is possible.

Disclosure: The author of this article is a paid contributor for CNN.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with reports from CNN and Politico, and the statement from Atty. Theodore J. Boutrous, Jr.

item.title: Why Treasury yields are ripping higher
item.description:
Data: FactSet; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips

Treasury yields are soaring, with the 30-year Treasury bond climbing to its highest level since 2004 Thursday.

  • The selloff in bonds started to accelerate Wednesday after a sizzling early report on the economy in September.

The big picture: For the bond market, these moves have been big. Bigly even.

  • On Thursday morning, the 30-year yield rose as high as 5.44%. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note was 5.13%.
  • Wednesday's gain of roughly 0.15 percentage point in the 10-year Treasury yield was the biggest since April 2025, when President Trump's "Liberation Day" tariff announcement rocked markets.

Flashback: Markets heads remember that it was ructions in the bond market — "They were getting yippy," the president famously said at the time — that prompted Trump to walk back some of the most extreme tariff policies.

Yes, but: This time, the dynamics driving the bond market are more complicated, global and difficult to manage.

  • Treasury yields have been moving higher for months on a combination of stronger-than-expected economic activity coupled with uncomfortably high inflation.
  • The surge in data center-related borrowing in the bond market is also pushing up interest rates, as tech borrowers compete with the U.S. Treasury for investor dollars.

Case in point: The big driver of Wednesday's surge in yields — which means, remember, that bond prices were falling — was one of the earliest economic reports on the U.S. economy in September.

  • These surveys of corporate purchasing managers suggested booming business in both the U.S. manufacturing and services industries. (JPMorgan economists said they were consistent with a 5% annual run rate for GDP growth.)
  • But they also showed that the prices these companies were paying were soaring as well. (In other words, more inflationary pressures are in the pipeline.)

Zoom out: Inflation is anathema for bond market investors as it erodes the value of the interest payments bondholders collect, making them less attractive assets.

  • The September survey data kicked off a wave of selling of Treasurys that rippled through the financial markets.
  • In the money markets — essentially very short-term bond markets — traders began to price in rising odds that Fed will have to pursue a serious cycle of rate hikes to get inflation under control.
  • The markets are now putting more than 50% odds on quarter-point increases at the Fed's October and December meeting.

Between the lines: Lurking in the background of the inflation-driven market move is the specter of a U.S. diesel export ban, which the Trump administration is reportedly considering.

  • But there's deep uncertainty about what such a ban would mean for overall inflation.
  • Some industry voices warn that such a ban could actually push prices of other refined products, like gasoline, sharply higher because of the way refineries operate.

What they're saying: "The proposed U.S. diesel export ban will not play out as the U.S. administration expects," wrote Susan Bell, an oil analyst with the consulting firm Rystad Energy. "While it may temporarily lower domestic diesel prices, it will cause the prices for all other refined products to soar as U.S. refineries cut run rates to balance their diesel production with the domestic demand."

  • "There is little flexibility to minimize diesel yield without cutting overall refinery throughput," Bell said.

The bottom line: The inflationary pressures appear to be building in the economy, which will be a headache both for politicians in the final stretch of the midterm elections and for policymakers like Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh.

item.title: Judge tosses Trump's lawsuit against Des Moines Register
item.description:
A district judge tossed an election interference lawsuit by President Trump against the Des Moines Register, parent company USA Today Co. (formerly Gannett) and pollster Ann Selzer, rejecting claims that its inaccurate pre-election poll amounted to consumer fraud.

Why it matters: The dismissal is an early court test of Trump's broader push to use litigation against media organizations over coverage he disputes.

  • Trump's lawyers say they will appeal.

Zoom in: In his ruling, Judge Scott Beattie said the plaintiff's attempt to use fraud law to allege liability on the poll was not a valid legal argument because political speech is protected by the First Amendment.

  • "As such, the only question before the Court is whether the Petition states a claim the law recognizes," Beattie wrote.
  • "At its core, the Plaintiffs' Petition seeks to stretch both Iowa statutory and common law beyond their current bounds, turning speech that enjoys the highest category of First Amendment protection into a liability."
  • "After considering the parties' arguments, the Court must conclude that the protection is too great and the reach is too far. The case must therefore be dismissed," he wrote.

What they're saying: "Today is a victory for the First Amendment—and for the essential role of a free press in American democracy. We are gratified that the Court recognized what this meritless lawsuit sought to obscure: that claims of "fake news" are little more than an attempt to punish news outlets for coverage those in power do not like," said Polly Grunfeld Sack, USA TODAY Co. chief legal counsel.

  • "A free press is fundamental to an informed public and a vibrant democracy. This decision reaffirms the enduring First Amendment principles that empower journalists and sends a message to those who think they can intimidate the press through legal action."

The other side: A spokesperson for Trump's legal team said the president would "take his powerful case to the Iowa Supreme Court," while repeating his allegations that the poll was intended to interfere in the election.

  • "Such fraud cannot be allowed to stand," the spokesperson said.

The big picture: The lawsuit is part of a broader effort by Trump and his administration to target media companies with legal action for what they believe is unfair coverage.

  • To date, the courts have mostly sided with media companies, citing the strength of the First Amendment.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with comments from Trump's legal team and to correct Judge Scott Beattie's last name.

item.title: Inside China's mind on AI
item.description:
China is waging a much different war for AI supremacy than the U.S.

Why it matters: China is obsessed with state control and adoption. Chinese officials are laser-focused on deep, widespread AI domestic use they can monitor and steer at every level of their economy.

  • By contrast, America is obsessed with developing superior AI faster. Period. The U.S. thinking: The nation first to true super-intelligence wins everything.

China and the U.S. agree on three AI certainties: The country with the most powerful AI holds power, sets global standards, and wins the coming decades economically and militarily.

From there, the two nations are on different roads. China's 15th Five-Year Plan, released in March, captures their strategy well.

  • AI appears 52 times, 5x more than a half-decade earlier. Computing power gets its own full chapter.
  • Their goal is clear: Integrate AI across 90% of the economy by 2030. America has nothing like this.

The bottom line: China doesn't get spooled up about white-collar job loss or humanity-ending rogue AI. The regime is worried most about AI turning against ... the regime.

  • Chen Yixin, China's spy chief, warned this month — in public — about AI's ability to launch public opinion wars and "cognitive warfare against China," threatening "political security, institutional security and ideological security."

China's weaknesses

China's AI strategy targets some substantial domestic problems they purposely omit in their AI sales pitch.

Why it matters: Americans tend to focus on China's growing strength — but much of its AI thinking flows from glaring weakness.

😱 They're staring down:

  • An aging population: China's population has shrunk for four years straight — and is very old. They have nearly as many people over 60 as America has in total. This helps explain their robotics obsession.
  • Very high youth unemployment: China's currently sits at 19%, basically double that of the U.S. — and an angry, young population with powerful AI tools is a threat to power.
  • Poor population outside major cities: This is a huge pain point. Then add in a five-year housing crisis, with prices falling for most people's most valuable asset.
  • Inferior chip production: Nvidia is simply way better than anything they've got. You can't compete on AI with uncompetitive chips — and Huawei, their Nvidia, is way behind despite state-directed help.
  • Export addiction: China is crushing it on exports, often flooding foreign markets with cheap cars, parts and technology. But its domestic economy is sucking wind — strong supply, weak demand.

China's strengths

China is America's only real AI competition — and, despite its weaknesses, it has some serious, structural advantages.

Why it matters: China leads in the physical ingredients for scaling AI: power, materials, robots and cheap models people actually use. These are the key ingredients for turning super-human intelligence into real economic and military power.

  • Think of it this way: If they catch up — or lap us — on AI capabilities and chip production, they're way better positioned to instantly impose and roll it out across society.

🦾 Their edge exists thanks to:

  • Power: Electricity is the biggest bottleneck on America's AI buildout, and China is swimming in it. BloombergNEF estimates China will add almost six times as much generating capacity as the U.S. over the next five years.
  • Vital materials: China dominates the minerals AI hardware runs on. The IEA tracks 20 essential ones for building AI and adjacent tech — and China dominates all but one, usually by huge margins. They have applied export controls to half of them as a way to slow us down.
  • Rolling out robots: This is where AI truly meets the real work. More than half of all industrial robots installed worldwide in 2024 went to China. They dominate us on this one. Better AI will equal better robots.
  • Cheap, widespread adoption: Chinese open-source models are the world's default for developers building cheaply. Five of the six most popular models on OpenRouter, a leading AI marketplace, come from Chinese firms.
  • Land-and-sky autonomy: They're simply crushing us on self-driving cars and self-flying drones. China's DJI alone has over 70% of the global drone market.

Understanding China's AI

China builds the world's best cheap open-source AI but trails America's most cutting-edge AI by about half a year, on a fraction of the investment.

  • That's the consensus of most AI experts we talk to. Truthfully, there's no rock-solid way to measure it, and every model release resets the estimates.

Why it matters: Everyone agrees on this: Chinese models are very good, gaining fast and are much cheaper to use.

The four you need to know:

  1. Kimi K3 (Moonshot): Widely rated as the best all-around open Chinese model. It's strongest on long, multi-step agentic tasks.
  2. Qwen3.8-Max (Alibaba): Also highly regarded and even tops some model rankings.
  3. GLM-5.3 (Zhipu / Z.ai): China's coding specialist. Its predecessor scored within a point of Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.8 on a key coding test, at under a fifth of the cost.
  4. DeepSeek V4 / V4.1-Flash: Among the cheapest to use. It's MIT-licensed and truly open.

The twist: U.S. officials and AI companies accuse Chinese labs of "distillation," covertly firing millions of questions at American models and training on the answers.

  • Washington has threatened sanctions and blacklisting, but hasn't pulled the trigger.

Worth noting: U.S. frontier labs have lately focused far more on building powerful lower-cost models to try to make sure Chinese AI can't undercut them on price.

Using it vs. fearing it

China is not big on dissent — or public opposition and hand-wringing about the regime's priorities.

  • That helps explain why the Chinese public is far more bullish on AI than America's.

Why it matters: They use it, like it and trust it — by wide margins.

  • 80% of Chinese people use AI weekly vs. 54% of Americans. It's in schools, public services and robots in hotels and stores.
  • 84% of Chinese people say AI excites them. That's the highest of any country. Only 38% of Americans say the same.
  • 87% of Chinese people trust AI, compared to just 32% of Americans. And 54% want more of it in daily life. That share is a measly 17% here.

Worth noting: Don't over-read it. ChinaTalk, a sharp China tracker, argues the optimism is overstated and masks rising worry about AI wiping out jobs.

item.content:encoded:
China is waging a much different war for AI supremacy than the U.S.

Why it matters: China is obsessed with state control and adoption. Chinese officials are laser-focused on deep, widespread AI domestic use they can monitor and steer at every level of their economy.

  • By contrast, America is obsessed with developing superior AI faster. Period. The U.S. thinking: The nation first to true super-intelligence wins everything.

China and the U.S. agree on three AI certainties: The country with the most powerful AI holds power, sets global standards, and wins the coming decades economically and militarily.

From there, the two nations are on different roads. China's 15th Five-Year Plan, released in March, captures their strategy well.

  • AI appears 52 times, 5x more than a half-decade earlier. Computing power gets its own full chapter.
  • Their goal is clear: Integrate AI across 90% of the economy by 2030. America has nothing like this.

The bottom line: China doesn't get spooled up about white-collar job loss or humanity-ending rogue AI. The regime is worried most about AI turning against ... the regime.

  • Chen Yixin, China's spy chief, warned this month — in public — about AI's ability to launch public opinion wars and "cognitive warfare against China," threatening "political security, institutional security and ideological security."

China's weaknesses

China's AI strategy targets some substantial domestic problems they purposely omit in their AI sales pitch.

Why it matters: Americans tend to focus on China's growing strength — but much of its AI thinking flows from glaring weakness.

😱 They're staring down:

  • An aging population: China's population has shrunk for four years straight — and is very old. They have nearly as many people over 60 as America has in total. This helps explain their robotics obsession.
  • Very high youth unemployment: China's currently sits at 19%, basically double that of the U.S. — and an angry, young population with powerful AI tools is a threat to power.
  • Poor population outside major cities: This is a huge pain point. Then add in a five-year housing crisis, with prices falling for most people's most valuable asset.
  • Inferior chip production: Nvidia is simply way better than anything they've got. You can't compete on AI with uncompetitive chips — and Huawei, their Nvidia, is way behind despite state-directed help.
  • Export addiction: China is crushing it on exports, often flooding foreign markets with cheap cars, parts and technology. But its domestic economy is sucking wind — strong supply, weak demand.

China's strengths

China is America's only real AI competition — and, despite its weaknesses, it has some serious, structural advantages.

Why it matters: China leads in the physical ingredients for scaling AI: power, materials, robots and cheap models people actually use. These are the key ingredients for turning super-human intelligence into real economic and military power.

  • Think of it this way: If they catch up — or lap us — on AI capabilities and chip production, they're way better positioned to instantly impose and roll it out across society.

🦾 Their edge exists thanks to:

  • Power: Electricity is the biggest bottleneck on America's AI buildout, and China is swimming in it. BloombergNEF estimates China will add almost six times as much generating capacity as the U.S. over the next five years.
  • Vital materials: China dominates the minerals AI hardware runs on. The IEA tracks 20 essential ones for building AI and adjacent tech — and China dominates all but one, usually by huge margins. They have applied export controls to half of them as a way to slow us down.
  • Rolling out robots: This is where AI truly meets the real work. More than half of all industrial robots installed worldwide in 2024 went to China. They dominate us on this one. Better AI will equal better robots.
  • Cheap, widespread adoption: Chinese open-source models are the world's default for developers building cheaply. Five of the six most popular models on OpenRouter, a leading AI marketplace, come from Chinese firms.
  • Land-and-sky autonomy: They're simply crushing us on self-driving cars and self-flying drones. China's DJI alone has over 70% of the global drone market.

Understanding China's AI

China builds the world's best cheap open-source AI but trails America's most cutting-edge AI by about half a year, on a fraction of the investment.

  • That's the consensus of most AI experts we talk to. Truthfully, there's no rock-solid way to measure it, and every model release resets the estimates.

Why it matters: Everyone agrees on this: Chinese models are very good, gaining fast and are much cheaper to use.

The four you need to know:

  1. Kimi K3 (Moonshot): Widely rated as the best all-around open Chinese model. It's strongest on long, multi-step agentic tasks.
  2. Qwen3.8-Max (Alibaba): Also highly regarded and even tops some model rankings.
  3. GLM-5.3 (Zhipu / Z.ai): China's coding specialist. Its predecessor scored within a point of Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.8 on a key coding test, at under a fifth of the cost.
  4. DeepSeek V4 / V4.1-Flash: Among the cheapest to use. It's MIT-licensed and truly open.

The twist: U.S. officials and AI companies accuse Chinese labs of "distillation," covertly firing millions of questions at American models and training on the answers.

  • Washington has threatened sanctions and blacklisting, but hasn't pulled the trigger.

Worth noting: U.S. frontier labs have lately focused far more on building powerful lower-cost models to try to make sure Chinese AI can't undercut them on price.

Using it vs. fearing it

China is not big on dissent — or public opposition and hand-wringing about the regime's priorities.

  • That helps explain why the Chinese public is far more bullish on AI than America's.

Why it matters: They use it, like it and trust it — by wide margins.

  • 80% of Chinese people use AI weekly vs. 54% of Americans. It's in schools, public services and robots in hotels and stores.
  • 84% of Chinese people say AI excites them. That's the highest of any country. Only 38% of Americans say the same.
  • 87% of Chinese people trust AI, compared to just 32% of Americans. And 54% want more of it in daily life. That share is a measly 17% here.

Worth noting: Don't over-read it. ChinaTalk, a sharp China tracker, argues the optimism is overstated and masks rising worry about AI wiping out jobs.
