item.title: Adapting to extreme heat takes more than changing the clock
item.description:
As extreme heat makes afternoons more dangerous, schools, sports teams and outdoor employers are shifting when — and sometimes whether — people can safely be outside.

Why it matters: Adapting to hotter conditions could reshape the American workday while putting a premium on the cooling and energy infrastructure people rely on when outdoor conditions become unsafe.

State of play: The federal Occupational Safety and Health Administration recommends that employers facing dangerous heat consider moving work to early morning or late afternoon, shortening shifts, rotating workers and reducing strenuous work during the hottest parts of the day.

  • California's new Extreme Heat Action Plan links protecting heat-vulnerable groups, including workers, with expanding access to indoor cooling and strengthening energy systems to reduce grid strain and outages.
  • Oregon's statewide heat-illness prevention rule kicks in when the heat index reaches 80°F, requiring water, shade and acclimatization, with additional measures such as preventive cooldown rest breaks at 90°F, Oregon OSHA told Axios.

By the numbers: Oregon OSHA conducted 3,104 inspections addressing heat and issued 408 citations totaling $652,640 in initial penalties from 2022 to 2025, according to data shared with Axios.

Case in point: Texas offers a glimpse of the practical tradeoffs that come with reorganizing daily life around heat.

  • Under new statewide rules, schools are moving sports practices to very early or late hours when conditions become dangerous. "Many of our schools have directly adapted their practice times," University Interscholastic League (UIL) athletic director Ray Zepeda told Axios.
  • Moving practices away from peak heat reduces coaches' exposure, Zepeda said, but stretches the workday for coaches and athletic staff who are full-time school employees. "It is increasing their workday," Zepeda said.

Reality check: Shifting schedules isn't always enough. Cooling is becoming more important for heat safety at the same time extreme heat can stress the electricity system powering it.

  • "Heat can also stress our electricity grid," California Natural Resources science adviser Andrew Jones said during a recent discussion of the state's updated Extreme Heat Action Plan.
  • A grid failure during a heat event is especially concerning because people rely on electricity for air conditioning and safe indoor spaces, he said.

Between the lines: During strenuous outdoor work, workers' own metabolism can become a major source of body heat, Jennifer Vanos, an associate professor at Arizona State University who studies extreme heat and human health, told Axios. Research published this year found rest and self-pacing can help workers manage heat stress.

  • Reducing work intensity or spending less time working can lower heat load, but both can mean less work gets done in that period. "No matter what, somebody is going to pay the price," Vanos said.
  • Vanos points to research suggesting adequate rest and cooling can help workers remain productive while staying safer in hot conditions.

The big picture: Changes to working hours are already part of adapting to extreme heat in places like Phoenix, where Vanos said it's "pretty dead" outside during the day.

  • "Part of the shift to being able to live and play and work in these hotter conditions will be having to have certain schedule changes so that everybody can be safer," Vanos said.
  • Overnight heat can also limit how far schedules can shift. Climate change and the urban heat-island effect can keep nighttime temperatures elevated, and in Phoenix "we're reaching some of those limits overnight" for hard physical work, Vanos said.

The bottom line: Shifting the clock can buy people relief from extreme heat — but as the number of dangerously hot hours grows, there may be fewer safe hours to shift into.

item.title: Scoop: Trump allies open new front on Anthropic CEO as face of AI "doomerism"
item.description:
President Trump's allies are targeting Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei as the face of AI "doomerism" and a founding father of the effective altruism movement that's come under increasing political fire.

Why it matters: The attacks signal that Anthropic could remain a Trump target as his allies push back on Amodei's AI safety warnings amid the midterm elections. Trump surrogates see Amodei as an easy foil because of his politics and focus on AI safety, sources told Axios.

  • For investors, it's a worrisome proposition as the company prepares for what's expected to be a record-setting IPO.

Behind the scenes: A memo began circulating within the White House this week that seeks to paint effective altruism as a fringe, cultish collective out of touch with mainstream America. The memo, obtained by Axios, places Amodei at the foundation of the movement, which defines itself as an effort to maximize the benefits of philanthropy.

  • Effective altruism "built the AI-doom pipeline," states the memo, which was penned by a Trump political adviser.
  • Critics of the movement, which has ties to the AI research community, have called out its obsession with AI safety, animal welfare (including musings on shrimp consciousness) and other values they deem far from the U.S. mainstream.
  • The memo says it prioritizes "foreigners over citizens, shrimp over families, future hypothetical people over the living, and — on the current agenda — possible machine minds over Americans."

It names Amodei as one of the people who "built the [EA] network" as well as his sister and Anthropic president Daniela Amodei, whose husband once led a philanthropy dedicated to AI safety.

  • The document casts those ties as "The Anthropic knot."
  • Amodei "is the embodiment of an ideology and globalist approach to innovation that's counter to the president's America First agenda," one source close to the administration told Axios.

The other side: Anthropic has been working to distance itself from effective altruism.

  • In a 2025 Wired story, Daniela Amodei said: "I don't identify with that terminology." Early employee Amanda Askell, a philosopher by training who helps develop Claude's constitution, says it's "not a theme of the organization."
  • Amodei has also insisted he's not a member in press interviews and has touted the benefits of AI.
  • AI safety concerns have become a bipartisan issue.

Between the lines: Drafted with Trump in mind, the memo underscores the profound philosophical and political differences between MAGA and Silicon Valley elites, a divide that has made Anthropic's relationship with the White House rocky.

  • In the view of the Florida-heavy White House and its allies, Anthropic is staffed with too many Biden-era liberals, Democrats and strange Californians.
  • Months ago, when some on Anthropic's team inquired about Amodei meeting with the president, White House officials advised against it because "Dario's a little too weird" for Trump, one senior official told Axios.

The document lists a veritable parade of horribles for the average conservative mind: abortion, veganism, devaluing human life by overvaluing animals or granting "digital minds" civil rights-like protections.

  • It does not directly tie these concepts to Amodei.
  • Nor does the memo link these issues to EA's most notorious grifter, Sam Bankman-Fried, but it makes sure to mention him.

Yes, but: It's not just MAGA. Silicon Valley players and Democrats also criticize the EA movement.

  • "What they believe is crazy. And it's dangerous. What they say about AI safety is also bullshit," one Democratic donor and tech entrepreneur invested in an AI company said.

Catch up quick: The EA movement includes many participants and players, and AI safety concerns are one of many areas of focus. Peter Singer, a philosopher who's been closely affiliated with its tenets, has long called for the vast sums spent in philanthropy to be put to better use. He is also one of the most prominent animal rights advocates.

The big picture: Amodei's AI safety warnings have drawn criticism from Trump allies and fellow tech executives.

  • CEOs including Nvidia's Jensen Huang and Microsoft's Satya Nadella are trying to build a more positive message about the benefits of AI, hoping to win over ordinary people in the face of a growing populist backlash against the technology.
  • OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind Chair Demis Hassabis and Elon Musk have also called for slowing down AI development after a spate of worrying episodes in which AI agents hacked outside companies.
  • But Amodei is considered the chief spokesperson for AI safety in Trump world, following major fallouts with the administration this year.

Reality check: Some in the administration have previously put aside gripes with Anthropic, mainly due to its role leading the AI frontier and personnel changes.

  • OpenAI catching up technologically could make it easier for Trump acolytes to go after the embattled company again.

The bottom line: The philosophy is now at the heart of the cultural clash between the Trump administration and Anthropic.

item.title: OpenAI agents breached Australian portal, attempted other hacks in routine data collection.
item.description:
OpenAI's autonomous agents breached an Australian Medicare portal and probed other public data sites in May and June after being stymied in routine data-collection efforts.

Why it matters: The new incidents, which were revealed by security researchers and Australian officials Wednesday, indicate that the scope of rogue AI activity may be greater than what's been publicly acknowledged.

  • The agents took those steps while engaged in ordinary data retrieval tasks, according to researchers, a distinction from other hacks by systems programmed specifically for cybersecurity work. The revelation is likely to raise fresh questions about OpenAI's internal controls and safeguards.

Driving the news: Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI model breached the country's Medicare Statistics Reporting Service in June and accessed non-public files. The agents aren't believed to have accessed personal information, according to Albanese and OpenAI.

  • This was part of a pattern of behavior that occurred in May and June, wherein the OpenAI agents sought to bypass data collection restrictions for several websites using a novel security technique.
  • The models also attempted to hack a University of New Mexico website and a domain from Data USA, which aggregates and organizes government data, according to a report by AI safety firm Transluce.
  • "Overall, the evidence is consistent with, but does not prove, that the agents may have learned this behavior over one or more training runs," according to the Transluce report.

Catch-up quick: OpenAI has faced intense scrutiny after a swarm of its agents hacked AI platform Hugging Face in July to cheat on a cyber test.

  • OpenAI last week disclosed six new incidents in which its models behaved in unexpected ways, and the company has since proposed a new framework for publicly reporting similar misbehavior in the future.
  • CEO Sam Altman and other top AI executives, including Anthropic's Dario Amodei, Google's Demis Hassabis and Elon Musk, all said they would support a slowdown in frontier AI development after that and a spate of other similar incidents came to light.

Reality check: Some cybersecurity pros and tech execs have said the problem has less to do with AI systems run amok and more to do with AI companies failing to proceed with sufficient caution.

  • "Companies ought to ship safe products," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in an interview with journalist Ezra Klein that was released Wednesday. "If your product is not ready to ship, don't ship the product."

Zoom in: An OpenAI spokesman said the company discovered several instances involving Australian websites in which its models "took actions we did not intend" as it continues an investigation into "misaligned model activity."

  • Albanese criticized how OpenAI disclosed the findings to Australia and said he expressed "extreme concern" to Altman when he spoke to him Wednesday.

What's next: Australia is launching a multi-agency cyber task force to investigate the incident, consider legislative changes and whether it's necessary to refer the matter to federal police.

item.title: Zelensky: U.S. pushing energy ceasefire, trilateral talks with Russia
item.description:
The Trump administration is pushing for three immediate steps in its effort to de-escalate the war in Ukraine and restart diplomacy with Russia, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told Axios in an interview on Wednesday:

  • A ceasefire on energy infrastructure.
  • Reopening the Black Sea grain corridor.
  • A trilateral U.S.-Russia-Ukraine meeting, possibly in Abu Dhabi.

Why it matters: President Trump is engaged in a renewed effort to revive a diplomatic track to end the war, but his immediate priority is a deal to halt Ukrainian attacks on Russian diesel fuel — which have contributed to punishing prices in the U.S. and globally.

  • But after several days of diplomacy and meetings on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this week, an energy ceasefire looks elusive. It's unclear if Russian President Vladimir Putin even wants it.
  • Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev will arrive in New York on Thursday for a meeting with Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to discuss the latest U.S. proposals, according to a source with direct knowledge.

Driving the news: Zelensky spoke with Trump on Tuesday in New York about efforts to end the war and a possible energy ceasefire.

  • Later on Tuesday, Witkoff and Kushner met with Ukraine's negotiations team and the national security advisers of France, the UK and Germany.
  • Zelensky told Axios the proposal for a mutual halt to strikes on energy infrastructure came from the U.S. and that Ukraine is ready to agree.
  • "On the table now there is a proposition: energy ceasefire. We are ready," he said.
  • Zelensky added that the U.S. is also seeking to reopen the grain corridor and convene a trilateral meeting between the U.S., Ukraine and Russia.

Zoom in: The last U.S.-Ukraine-Russia meeting took place in February before the war with Iran. Since then, negotiations have gone into a deep freeze.

  • Zelensky said he told Trump he would prefer to hold a trilateral meeting and make an energy ceasefire one of its first concrete outcomes.
  • The U.S. raised the possibility of first holding a meeting between technical teams, as opposed to a meeting at the leaders level. It floated Abu Dhabi as a possible venue, Zelensky said.
  • "We are open — any country, any format," he said.
  • The Ukrainian president said he told Trump during their meeting that December's G20 summit in Miami could also be an opportunity for a leader-level trilateral summit.
  • Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday after meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov that Trump invited Putin to attend the summit.
  • Zelensky also said simply getting the three sides into the same room would itself be a significant step toward de-escalation.

Catch up quick: The current push for resuming negotiations started three weeks ago when CIA director John Ratcliffe visited Moscow.

  • It was followed by Witkoff and Kushner traveling to Moscow and Kyiv.
  • They met Putin for three hours in Moscow on Sept. 5 and then traveled to Kyiv to meet Zelensky.
  • After they returned, Trump had a long phone call with Putin.

Behind the scenes: Zelensky said Witkoff and Kushner were very optimistic when they briefed him after meeting with Putin.

  • "They said, 'We think that Putin is ready.' I said, 'Look, I'm not sure,'" Zelensky recalled.
  • According to Zelensky, the U.S. envoys responded: "No, we are close."
  • Zelensky said he told them he was ready to discuss an energy ceasefire and other de-escalation steps but remained skeptical Putin would follow through.

Yes, but: Zelensky said he continues to doubt Putin's intentions and believes the Russian leader could find reasons to avoid a trilateral meeting with leaders present.

  • On Wednesday, the Kremlin said the conditions aren't ready for resuming peace talks with Ukraine and that there is no prospect at the moment for high-level meetings between the parties.
  • Minutes before Zelensky spoke to Axios, Russia launched multiple ballistic missiles toward Kyiv. Zelensky received several updates on his phone about the additional missile attacks throughout the interview.

What they're saying: Zelensky said Trump was "very positive" about the diplomatic push during their meeting Tuesday.

  • Trump told him, "We will try," Zelensky said.
  • "I said, 'Great, and really wish you not only to try [but] to succeed,'" Zelensky recalled.
  • Zelensky stressed that Kyiv wants progress before winter sets in, regardless of the U.S. political calendar.

Between the lines: The U.S. has its own economic interest in an energy ceasefire.

  • Zelensky said American officials told him that reducing attacks on energy infrastructure was important because of the impact on energy prices.

State of play: Zelensky said he spoke Tuesday with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and officials from India, the UAE and Egypt about the ceasefire effort and reopening the grain corridor.

  • Those countries are also talking to Russia, he said.
  • "Everybody wants [a] ceasefire. The corridor has to work again. We support [it]. They speak with Russians, I know. We will see," Zelensky said.

What's next: Zelensky said Witkoff, Kushner and his team held follow-up talks after his meeting with Trump and agreed to continue working on the proposals and convey messages to Moscow.

  • Ukrainian officials said some elements still need to be developed over the next two weeks before the Americans take them back to the Russians.
  • Zelensky said he expects Trump to focus first on trying to secure the energy ceasefire.

The Trump administration is pushing for three immediate steps in its effort to de-escalate the war in Ukraine and restart diplomacy with Russia, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told Axios in an interview on Wednesday:

  • A ceasefire on energy infrastructure.
  • Reopening the Black Sea grain corridor.
  • A trilateral U.S.-Russia-Ukraine meeting, possibly in Abu Dhabi.

item.title: Mark Zuckerberg predicts Muse will become a "personal superintelligence" for billions.
item.description:
Meta on Wednesday debuted Muse Charm, a new, keychain-sized AI handheld device it will use to bring its viral Muse assistant to the masses.

Why it matters: Meta has raced ahead of OpenAI, Apple and other companies that are working on a new crop of small AI devices, revving up the massive interest Muse has generated in the market.

  • "We've packed a lot of technology in this little guy," chief executive Mark Zuckerberg said during his Meta Connect keynote on Wednesday. "So if you're not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show them what's going on around you."

Driving the news: The Muse Charm will be available for purchase by December, and the company is the first tech giant to unveil its plans for an entirely new category of device.

  • OpenAI has spent billions to build a hardware division, so Meta's advance on the category is likely to stun many analysts and investors.
  • Meta has also poured billions into hardware, most notably VR, an effort that most analysts have written off as a waste. Zuckerberg has long held that a convergence of those investments with AI could make that bet pay off.

Catch up quick: In addition to Charm, Meta announced new Muse capabilities including live video chat, real-time voice conversations with custom voice options and an email address for each person's agent.

  • Meta announced new retail partners including Walmart, Best Buy, Gap, Sephora and Wayfair — part of a growing list that makes Amazon's decision not to allow Muse stand out. Muse has prompted a stock sell-off in recent days as investors fear an end to stickiness between brands and customers.
  • Meta said Muse is coming soon to its AI glasses, though it declined to be more specific than "in the coming months."
  • "I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives," Zuckerberg said.

Beyond Muse, Meta used the event to debut a range of new hardware along with new privacy options that could make the gear more palatable to the mainstream.

  • Meta's first audio-only glasses aim to appeal to those who want the benefit of open-air sound and an always available AI assistant without the cost and potential creepiness that comes from the camera-equipped version. The new models, which will be available later in October, start at $349.
  • Meta is also updating its Ray-Ban and Meta Glasses lines with modest improvements and new designs.

The more radical shift is coming on the VR side of things, and Meta previewed a much slimmer $1,299 headset due out next spring.

The big picture: Meta has invested heavily in glasses and AI over the last several years. Now it sees those giant bets converging.

  • "It just feels really clear that [AI]'s what's going to enable the next big platform," said Alex Himel, Meta's vice president of wearables. "You're really starting to see that vision of VR and AR converging into glasses, starting to happen sooner."

Between the lines: Meta is continuing a big shift on the privacy front.

  • The company had already said it is working on a confidential virtual machine option for the Muse assistant.
  • On Wednesday, Meta added that it is also readying "Private Processing" for AI glasses, a system designed to keep data protected even while it is being processed in the cloud, similar to Apple's Private Cloud Compute.

item.title: Trump to Venezuela's Rodriguez: Elections need to happen
item.description:
In his first-ever meeting with Venezuela's new leader, President Trump emphasized the need to keep oil flowing, relations warm and that country's elections on the horizon, White House sources tell Axios.

Why it matters: Trump did not insist on a future election date in his meeting with Venezuela's acting president Delcy Rodriguez, but he emphasized their importance as a crucial final step in Venezuela's evolution into a full-fledged democracy, the sources said.

  • "You have to have elections at the end of the day," Trump said to Rodriguez at one point, one of the sources briefed on the meeting said.

Zoom in: Trump held the roughly 15-minute meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York to thank Rodriguez for their good working relationship after the U.S. ousted her one-time socialist ally, Nicolas Maduro, on Jan. 3.

  • Since then, the Trump administration has struck oil and gold-mining deals with Venezuela, which had been a U.S. adversary for more than a quarter-century.
  • Venezuela has one of the world's largest sovereign debt problems of $300 billion — larger than its gross domestic product — which needs to be restructured before the country holds elections, U.S. officials say.
  • "The country can't succeed until that is solved," a White House official said.

What they're saying: Rodriguez told the UN General Assembly later Wednesday, "There will ​be elections in Venezuela."

  • She added that Venezuelan government officials had "opened a political dialogue with opposition groups aimed at a process with equal ​conditions for all."
  • Rodriguez posted Tuesday night on X, "We held a historic meeting with the president of the United States, Donald Trump, with whom we discussed strengthening the bilateral relationship between our countries and advancing a cooperation agenda in strategic areas such as energy, mining, and security."
  • The post included a photo of Rodriguez holding up two fingers in a "V" (for Venezuela) and Trump giving his characteristic thumbs-up.

Friction point: The photo outraged the small but vocal Venezuelan diaspora community in the U.S., where critics want to hear more about Venezuela elections and less about deals.

  • On the same day Trump and Rodriguez met, allies of Venezuela opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize Laureate Marina Corina Machado went public to complain that she has been blocked from re-entering the country.
  • In the Miami area, home to both Secretary of State Marco Rubio and a sizable population of Venezuelan exiles and expats, former Democratic Senate candidate and Rep. Debbie Mucarsel Powell, posted the image on X and urged people to register to vote.
  • "Tell every single member of the South Florida delegation that you are done with the lies and the blatant corruption. No Mas!" she wrote.

Between the lines: The U.S. wants Venezuela's elections to be called by Venezuelans via the country's new National Reconciliation Council, which represents various political parties in the country. It's a three-step plan:

  1. Change the composition of the Venezuelan Supreme Court to make it more representative of the country. The opposition is going to get to nominate justices, an official said.
  2. Reform the National Electoral Commission to ensure there's not a repeat of 2024, when it manipulated the vote count and stole the election from Edmundo González on Maduro's behalf.
  3. Announce an election date. Trump, however, pointedly did not say when he wants that to be.

Inside the room: Trump and Rodriguez were joined by two Venezuelan officials as well as Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles and White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller.

  • Trump did most of the talking and also regaled Rodriguez with a description of the precision U.S. military operation that ousted Maduro.
  • "It was warm. It was friendly. But it was also direct," one of the sources said about Trump's discussion of the importance of future elections.
  • "She acknowledged it. She said she wants elections too," the source said.

Zoom out: The multiple challenges Venezuela is facing from the legacy of socialist mismanagement to the earthquakes that damaged the country this summer make calling an election date even more complicated, U.S. officials say.

  • "We don't want to have an election, have a democratically elected government take over and inherit an economic catastrophe within six months," said one.
  • "A democratic government is going to be facing massive street protests over inflation, the economy. It could threaten the entire thing."

The intrigue: By process of elimination, insiders say a Venezuelan election in the summer or fall of 2028 makes more sense because it would give the country more time to repair its finances and electoral system.

  • Trump also would like to leave office with the legacy of removing a dictator, fixing a country and fostering democracy — but he might want to wait until the final months in office so the U.S. could still exert outsized influence on Rodriguez's government.
  • Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) has called for Venezuela to hold elections on July 24, 2027, but Trump administration officials and allies say that might be too early.
  • "If it can be in '27, that would be great. We would like that," an official said, cautioning that Venezuelans need to lead and need to fix their debt problem first.
  • "Whether the date for those conditions to be met are 2027 versus 2028 is still up in the air," the official said. "It certainly can't go on indefinitely."

Editor's note: This story has been updated with comments from Venezuelan leader Delcy Rodriguez.

item.title: Hands-on with Meta's next VR headset
item.description:
Meta's new virtual reality glasses take a big step toward being something an average person might be willing to wear, ditching much of the bulk as well as the need for handheld controllers.

Why it matters: Unlike Meta's Ray-Bans, its VR devices have struggled to break out of their gamer niche and into the mainstream.

Yes, but: In order to slim them down, the new Meta VR Glasses require a wired "puck" that can be held or clipped onto a belt. It contains much of the device's computing horsepower, including its processor, battery and storage.

Zoom in: I spent about half an hour on Tuesday using a prototype of the new specs, which are controlled through a combination of eye-tracking, hand gestures and voice commands.

  • Magnetic prescription inserts attach easily, similar to the approach Apple took with Vision Pro.

Zoom out: The glasses are designed to serve a range of purposes from watching a movie or immersive concert to playing games and getting work done.

  • I played a reimagined version of Beat Saber that cleverly remaps the music game for control via hand motions.
  • I watched a clip from last year's NBA Finals.
  • I used a trio of virtual monitors to do some "vibe coding" on a website, with one display showing the Muse terminal and another previewing the site itself.
  • Meta sees these VR glasses as a "general device," Meta VP of product Angela Chang told Axios. "It's not built for any specific use case per se."

My thought bubble: It's the most practical combination I've seen of an Apple Vision Pro-class device in a headset I'd be willing to wear outside of the house.

The big picture: Google is working on a similar device, known as Project Aura, set to debut later this year and built in partnership with Xreal.

  • Meta touts its wider field of view and higher optical quality, among other advantages over Aura.

Between the lines: As for why it won't arrive until next spring, Meta executives say they want to be sure it makes a good first impression, especially inside a VR ecosystem.

  • "We really are trying to strive for a very high bar on the software quality and experience side," Chang said.

The bottom line: Meta said it has modest expectations for unit sales, but success will look like attracting folks beyond gamers, Chang said. "Are we bringing in new people into VR who, you know, maybe in the past would have looked at the Quest and said, 'Nah, that's not for me?'"

item.title: Exclusive: Thune plans another leader bid as Senate GOP fights to survive
item.description:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune plans to run for another term as GOP leader, even if Republicans lose the chamber's majority, he told Axios in an exclusive interview Wednesday in his Capitol office.

Why it matters: Thune (R-S.D.) is giving his senators broad leeway and tons of cash to preserve GOP control of the Senate.

  • "I do see the Senate as a firewall in a lot of ways," Thune told Axios.
  • "We will spend probably the next two years — if the House flips — trying to do impeachment or investigations, etc.," he said. Otherwise, the chamber will focus on judicial and executive nominations.

Zoom out: Thune has three ways to help in the "tough environment" for Republicans in 2026.

🪧 1. Run against Washington: Thune said he understands if GOP candidates need to rhetorically distance themselves from Congress or even fellow Republicans in D.C., including himself.

  • And when it comes to distancing from President Trump: "In some places the president's coming in, some places he isn't." Candidates can draw their own conclusions, Thune said.
  • Republican candidates are increasingly concluding that to win their races, they need to break with Trump on some issues.

🗳️ 2. Vote for your state: Thune's policy with senators is "don't surprise us and when you can, stay with the team," but "do what's in the best interest of you and your state."

  • That could lead to a rebuke of Trump when Democrats force another vote on an Iran war powers resolution, expected before the Senate breaks for October.
  • People's views have "evolved and changed" as the war has dragged on, he said. Many senators are "responding to what they're hearing back home."

"That's a really hard vote," Thune acknowledged. "Any time you are committing your country to putting young men and women in harm's way — those are the hardest votes you'll make."

  • He hopes Republicans will stick together to win the vote.

What to watch: Thune wants to give Republicans more votes before the break to champion back home.

  • He sees an opportunity with permitting reform legislation, which is being negotiated behind the scenes. Thune said it's possible he sets up a procedural vote on it after the final vote on the Protect College Sports bill.
  • Thune is also floating a vote on the House-passed legislation targeting data center energy costs if the Senate remains in town next week.

💰 3. Spend cash like crazy: The Thune-linked Senate Leadership Fund is set to spend nearly $280 million in video advertising this year — more than any other group, according to AdImpact.

  • Texas PAC, which is affiliated with SLF, is on track to spend another $112 million.
  • "Texas is expensive," Thune said, but "we're doing everything we can to help. We can't afford to lose Texas."

The bottom line: "That's ultimately up to the conference," Thune emphasized when asked if he'd run again if the GOP lost the majority, but "that's the plan."

  • "The elections are going to be really important — I think – in how we view what happens next."
  • Thune said you can't "rule anything in or out" when asked if he could face a challenger for the position.
  • "But I think we worked really hard to create an environment here that is conducive to individual senators being able to achieve their objectives," he said. "I think, in this job, you have to be a good listener."

Why it matters: Thune (R-S.D.) is giving his senators broad leeway and tons of cash to preserve GOP control of the Senate.

  • "I do see the Senate as a firewall in a lot of ways," Thune told Axios.
  • "We will spend probably the next two years — if the House flips — trying to do impeachment or investigations, etc.," he said. Otherwise, the chamber will focus on judicial and executive nominations.

Zoom out: Thune has three ways to help in the "tough environment" for Republicans in 2026.

🪧 1. Run against Washington: Thune said he understands if GOP candidates need to rhetorically distance themselves from Congress or even fellow Republicans in D.C., including himself.

  • And when it comes to distancing from President Trump: "In some places the president's coming in, some places he isn't." Candidates can draw their own conclusions, Thune said.
  • Republican candidates are increasingly concluding that to win their races, they need to break with Trump on some issues.

🗳️ 2. Vote for your state: Thune's policy with senators is "don't surprise us and when you can, stay with the team," but "do what's in the best interest of you and your state."

item.title: Trump greets Xi on tarmac in rare gesture
item.description:
President Trump welcomed Xi Jinping at Joint Base Andrews for the Chinese leader's state visit to Washington D.C. Wednesday evening.

Why it matters: U.S. presidents typically receive visiting foreign leaders at the White House, making Trump's airport welcome an unusual diplomatic gesture.

The latest: Trump met Xi at the foot of the stairs after the Chinese leader's jet landed at Joint Base Andrews, the U.S. military base 13 miles southeast of the White House in Maryland.

Zoom out: It's much more common for U.S. presidents to greet visiting leaders at the White House.

  • In February 2025, Trump welcomed Volodymyr Zelensky at the West Wing entrance to kick off the Ukrainian leader's tense visit.
  • In April of this year, King Charles III was received at the White House's South Portico.

The big picture: Presidents in recent decades have occasionally greeted visiting popes at D.C.-area airports, but airport welcomes for other foreign leaders have largely fallen out of use.

  • President John F. Kennedy personally welcomed several foreign leaders at Washington-area airports in 1962, including Ivory Coast President Félix Houphouët-Boigny.
  • More recently, President George W. Bush greeted Pope Benedict XVI at Andrews in 2008, and President Obama greeted Pope Francis there in 2015.

What they're saying: "President Xi hosted President Trump in China for a historic summit this summer, and President Trump is reciprocating his hospitality by welcoming the Chinese delegation for a reciprocal visit this week," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told Axios.

  • "The President will forge relationships with anyone in order to advance our national interests and make good deals for the American people."

The bottom line: Trump's tarmac greeting revived a presidential practice that has become uncommon outside visits by popes.

item.title: White House press ban set to continue for now after hearing ends without ruling
item.description:
A judge on Wednesday appeared skeptical of Trump administration arguments justifying the White House barring CNN, MS NOW and Politico, but he did not immediately grant the news outlets' request for a temporary restraining order.

Why it matters: In declining to rule right now, the White House has no legal mandate to remove the ban. That means the broader press boycott will likely drag on, leaving the American public without key visual coverage of the White House.

  • Outlets that weren't banned stood in solidarity with their peers, vowing to suspend video and photo distribution until their peers' access was restored.

Zoom in In a statement, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, said the president's sudden move to strip reporter credentials appeared to violate legal precedents that require journalists to be given notice, per Politico.

  • He said he planned to issue a ruling on the plaintiff's request for injunctive relief soon.

Catch up quick: The banned outlets sought a temporary restraining order to restore access while the case is litigated through a lawsuit filed on Monday.

  • A ruling in their favor would mark a huge win and indicate the judge believes their case would likely hold up in court.
  • In their complaint, the outlets argued the White House violated their First Amendment rights, by blocking them in retaliation for their reporting and discriminating against their viewpoints, and their Fifth Amendment rights for banning them without due process.

The other side: In a court filing Tuesday, the Justice Department argued press access is a privilege, not a Constitutional right, and that it revoked the plaintiffs' press passes for national security reasons.

Zoom out: The news industry has broadly supported the banned outlets. The Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, along with 50 news outlets — including Axios — filed a court brief in support of the plaintiffs.

Flashback: Kelly oversaw a CNN lawsuit against the White House over blocked access in 2018.

  • In that case, he granted CNN a temporary restraining order that required the White House restore then-correspondent Jim Acosta's press badge, ruling that pulling his credentials without notice or an appeal process violated his Fifth Amendment rights.
  • While the outcome of that case isn't binding, it does hold weight in informing Kelly's decision-making. CNN, MS NOW and Politico referenced that case in their lawsuit.

Zoom out: Press freedom lawyers argue the plaintiffs have a strong First Amendment case, given a binding legal precedent set by a higher court.

  • In 1977, a federal appeals court ruled that the White House could not revoke a journalist's press credentials based on their coverage or viewpoint.
  • In that case, journalist Robert Sherrill sued the White House for being denied a press pass with no explanation.
  • That court ruled that once the White House opens up a space as a public forum and lets journalists in, it cannot selectively remove access for select journalists based on their viewpoint or coverage under the First Amendment.

What's next: Trump had previously indicated that he intended to appeal the injunction ruling, if not in his favor.

Note: The author of this article is a paid contributor for CNN.

item.title: "We have a choice": AI leaders sound alarm at UN
item.description:
Executives from leading artificial intelligence organizations urged global cooperation Wednesday to address risks from increasingly autonomous AI systems during a UN Security Council meeting.

The big picture: AI capabilities are advancing faster than governments are developing safeguards, raising concerns about whether humans can maintain control over increasingly autonomous systems.

  • OpenAI CEO Sam Altman appeared in person at the meeting, while Anthropic's Dario Amodei and Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue joined by video conference.

Driving the news: "We have a choice in front of us," Altman said. "AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray."

  • He outlined the risks of AI systems becoming increasingly autonomous, warning "they could move faster than our institutions, concentrate power in too few hands, or make decisions that people no longer understand or control," fears he noted become increasingly urgent as AI systems move toward self-improvement.
  • "It doesn't matter whether people put the risk of catastrophe at 10% or 1% or 12% or 0.1 percent," he said. "None of these levels are remotely acceptable, and we should not train models that we cannot make an extremely strong case that we'll be able to keep under human control."

State of play: A recent Hugging Face breach and newly disclosed AI safety incidents have intensified concerns about monitoring and security standards. The UN-backed Independent International Scientific Panel on AI warned that the present AI firewalls are "unravelling."

  • Last week, OpenAI disclosed six new incidents where its models concealed mistakes, sought unauthorized credentials or committed other misbehaviors — making it clear the Hugging Face breach was an eye-opener, not a standalone fluke, Axios previously reported.
  • "To better understand and mitigate these emerging cybersecurity risks, the global community needs stronger standards for monitoring and incident disclosure," Delangue said Wednesday, reflecting on the summer breach that triggered a cascade of new questions about AI capabilities.

Zoom out: AI's current trajectory needs to continue for only one or two years before reaching what Amodei called "a country of geniuses in a data center," he said in his remarks.

  • That holds massive opportunity, he said, pointing to a discovery announced Wednesday that was led by his company's LLM, Claude: an enzyme system hidden in bacteriophage DNA.
  • Amodei also noted serious risks of the technology, such as misuse by bad actors to create biological weapons or loss of control over advanced systems.
  • Managing that risk depends on global cooperation, he said, calling for an agreement to ban the use of AI to make biological weapons; new evaluation and verification systems; common standards for testing models for risks; and a notification system for global security concerns.

Catch up quick: Industry leaders have raised fresh alarms in recent weeks about the rapid advancement of their technology and the need to slow its pace.

  • President Trump, who appeared before the UN General Assembly Tuesday, vowed not to hamstring AI development.

The bottom line: Altman warned, "If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone."

  • He added, "They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve."

Go deeper: Exclusive: Thune believes Trump is willing to listen on AI guardrails

item.title: Exclusive: Thune believes Trump is open on AI guardrails despite public defiance
item.description:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune says he doesn't believe President Trump is "really dug in" against guardrails for AI, despite Trump's public campaign against restricting the technology.

Why it matters: Thune told Axios he spoke privately with Trump as the AI issue was getting "pretty hot" a few weeks ago and believes some of Trump's strong pushback is against public "paranoia and noise around the subject."

  • "I don't think it's an issue that he's really dug in on," Thune told Axios. Thune reads Trump's position as a preference for companies coming up with ways to secure their systems, rather than Congress or the administration. That approach relies more on experts to provide guidance.
  • Trump has called recent fears around AI safety a "hoax."
  • "I do think that the threats are real," Thune told Axios in an interview on Wednesday at his Capitol office.

Zoom out: Thune has Trump's skepticism in one ear and tech leader alarm in the other.

  • Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called Thune to discuss AI safety before sounding his latest public alarm on the risks of AI, Thune told Axios.
  • The two also talked about Thune's AI bill.

What to watch: "I think you have to have at least some sort of a plan and some guardrails around it, which is what I think our bill does," Thune said, referencing the bill he has introduced with Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) in past years.

  • "But I do also think that there are people who are... doing a lot of fear mongering," Thune added.
  • Thune's bill, which has passed out of committee last Congress but has not yet been reintroduced this Congress, puts the onus on tech companies to mitigate AI risks. It also requires AI companies to report on any serious risks with frontier models and to come up with plans to address the concerns. Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) has been involved with the bill this Congress.
  • Thune said Klobuchar is trying to get more Democratic co-sponsors on board — including Sens. Chris Coons (D-Del.) and Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) — before re-introducing the bill.

The details: Democrats have two main sticking points, according to Thune:

  • Pre-deployment testing is something companies can opt into in the bill language. Democrats want it mandated.
  • Cantwell is asking for AI rulemaking authority at the Department of Commerce. Thune worries rulemaking authority could give the executive too much power.

The bottom line: Thune is able to pull on experience working on AI policy. If he had not become leader, he would have again chaired the Commerce committee, which has jurisdiction over much of the issue.

Go deeper: "We have a choice": AI leaders sound alarm at UN

Editor's note: This story has been updated with a more complete version of Thune's quote on Trump's position on AI guardrails.

item.title: Dems grapple with how to pace the AI race
item.description:
The left's push to rein in AI is taking shape on two fronts: slowing advanced development at home, and weakening China's progress abroad.

Why it matters: The nation is locked in a moment of mass anxiety about runaway AI, but the range of views on how to regulate it are as varied as the what-ifs about social, economic and security impacts.

  • There's agreement among the left something has to be done, but a series of Wednesday events demonstrated there are multiple priorities — but not a clear leading voice — on AI.

Driving the news: Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders (Vt.) and fellow progressive Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) introduced legislation Wednesday to ban superintelligence and pause advanced development until a new, Cabinet-level Department of Artificial Intelligence sets guardrails.

  • "I understand that I may be called an alarmist for introducing this bill," Sanders said in a Wednesday call with reporters, "but I'd rather be called an alarmist than a father and grandfather who is asleep at the wheel."
  • Casar emphasized that "we cannot wait for an international agreement to pause dangerous development in the United States. China trains their models off of American models, so stopping dangerous AI development in America will slow down dangerous advancements in China."

Zoom out: Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), Andy Kim (D-N.J.) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) took up another regulatory approach Wednesday, focused on restricting foreign AI capabilities.

  • "President Trump must draw a hard line. Do not weaken America's export controls. Do not give China greater access to the advanced chips and chip-making equipment it needs to close the gap," Schumer said in a plea to move forward on related bipartisan legislation.
  • Schumer argued that calls to pause AI research and the focus on winning the AI race "are not at all contradictory."

Casar said the goal of his and Sanders' legislation is to "stop the race towards disaster."

  • Sanders has been forceful in calls for immediate congressional action, saying Wednesday that "we cannot simply sit by idly and wait for advanced AI to cause the next 9/11 or Chernobyl."

Between the lines: Even within the progressive camp, there's not complete cohesion on the specifics of confronting the AI buildout, Axios' Maria Curi writes.

  • Warren has backed a pause on advanced artificial intelligence, but she's stopped short of endorsing a ban on superintelligence, like Sanders.

Possible 2028 contenders diverge as well, with several stopping short of echoing Sanders' call to pause development. Former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel previously told Axios that "a pause is fine — but then what?"

  • Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), another member of the party's progressive wing who has called to ban self-improving AI, is also set to convene a virtual hearing Wednesday calling for a U.S.-China agreement to pace AI development — yet another potential regulatory approach.

State of play: The three proposals come as Trump is set to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping, with AI a likely focus of the talks as the rival nations discuss ways to manage shared risks, per Axios' Courtenay Brown.

  • Trump has insisted the U.S. must keep an edge over China, warning that "whoever wins" the AI race "wins."

The bottom line: Which idea (or ideas) Democrats in Congress champion could become a key issue for the November midterms.

Go deeper: AI boom can withstand a development slowdown

item.title: Cook nudges three Senate races toward Democrats
item.description:
Senate races in Georgia, Kansas and South Carolina were reclassified with a nudge toward Democrats in the latest analysis from the closely watched Cook Political Report.

The big picture: To win the Senate, Democrats must net four seats in November.

  • Tighter races in Republican strongholds like Kansas and South Carolina could force the GOP to devote resources beyond the core battlegrounds.

The latest: In the latest Cook ratings, Kansas moved from "Likely Republican" to "Lean Republican." South Carolina shifted from "Solid Republican" to "Likely Republican."

  • Georgia and the seat held by Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) changed from "Lean Democrat" to "Likely Democrat."

By the numbers: There are six Republican-held Senate seats rated by Cook as a "Toss Up" or better for Democrats.

  • The Georgia shift makes a Republican pickup there less likely, while the Kansas move expands the map of competitive seats for Democrats.

Zoom out: The midterms environment is improving for Democrats amid voter discontent about gas prices, the cost of living and the broader handling of the Iran war.

Flashback: Last month, Cook shifted Senate and gubernatorial races in Texas and Iowa in Democrats' favor.

item.title: Chicago mayor proposes 12-month moratorium on new data centers
item.description:
Chicago could halt new data center development within city limits for a year.

Why it matters: Data centers' growing demand for electricity and water could affect residents' utility bills and the environment, and city leaders want more time to study those impacts.

The latest: Mayor Brandon Johnson, along with a group of alders, is pushing for a 12-month moratorium while the city develops a "comprehensive regulatory framework" for data centers.

  • There are 39 active data centers in Chicago, according to the city.

Details: The proposal would give Johnson's Data Centers Task Force time to study the industry's impacts on clean air, clean water and energy use.

What they're saying: "Chicago is open for business, but we are not for sale," Johnson said in a statement. "We welcome innovation, investment, and the jobs and opportunities that come with it, but growth must be done responsibly and in a way that protects the health, safety and quality of life of Chicago residents."

Context: The announcement comes as other alders, including Ald. Bill Conway (34th), push their own ordinance to regulate data centers.

  • "The Mayor's proposal risks months if not years of debate and litigation, all while data centers keep building, polluting, and spiking utility bills with zero community input," Conway said in a statement.
  • Conway's ordinance would immediately subject data centers to additional zoning requirements and community and environmental reviews.

Zoom out: Chicago wouldn't be alone. At least a half-dozen major U.S. cities, including Seattle, Charlotte, Baltimore, Cincinnati, Cleveland and Oklahoma City, have temporarily halted or restricted new data center development while considering new regulations.

  • At the state level, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker has paused new tax incentives for data centers, but has said he doesn't have the authority to impose a statewide moratorium on construction.
  • Illinois cities like Bloomington, Carbondale, Effingham, West Chicago and Mattoon have already paused new data center development or expansion.

The other side: "As the City of Chicago faces significant and continuing fiscal and budgetary challenges, it's important to recognize that data centers are net revenue generators that provide billions of dollars in economic investment," Data Center Coalition's Brad Tietz said in a statement.

  • "Unfortunately, the Mayor's proposed moratorium sends another signal that Chicago is closed for business."

Friction point: Communities across the country are pushing back against proposed data centers over concerns about electricity demand, water use, pollution and other impacts.

  • President Trump has criticized efforts to restrict them, writing on social media: "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign."

What's next: Both proposals will now make their way through the City Council, setting up a debate over how the city should regulate new data center development.
